items.text:
Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security.
Albanese has been one of Israel’s foremost critics, documenting its genocidal war on Gaza as well as its systematic discrimination against Palestinians and illegal settlement in occupied Palestinian territory since 1967.
Albanese was stopped by police on security grounds on Thursday as she arrived at Juan Santamaria international airport in the capital San Jose, where she was due to be presented with an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica.
Albanese, who called the move “a disgrace”, was still being held at the airport on Friday.
Omer Badilla, the director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, later appeared to offer some explanation on social media, saying Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”, without specifying the nature of that alert or which country had issued it.
“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here,” Badilla continued without elaborating. “Our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system.”
While the move was welcomed by Israel, including by its Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, a number of Costa Rican and regional figures and rights groups, as well as the University of Costa Rica, have objected to the treatment of Albanese and demanded an explanation.
On Thursday, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (AJUFIDH) urged the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to seek answers from the Costa Rican government, arguing that the ban may violate international obligations protecting UN experts.
Costa Rican lawmakers from several political parties have also criticised the move, describing it as arbitrary and damaging to the country’s reputation for defending human rights and international law, while the university has formally requested that immigration authorities and foreign ministry officials explain the legal grounds for the decision.
Why would Israel celebrate a UN figure not being allowed entry to Costa Rica?
As Special Rapporteur, Albanese has used her position to document Israeli violations of international law. She accuses Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, maintaining an apartheid system against Palestinians and pursuing territorial expansion through illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.
In her March 2024 report, Anatomy of a Genocide, for which she received numerous threats, Albanese found that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that Israel had committed acts prohibited under the UN Genocide Convention. She subsequently called for an arms embargo, sanctions against Israel and an end to the trade and financial relationships sustaining its occupation.
Throughout her tenure, Albanese has repeatedly described the occupation of Palestinian territory as an entrenched system of apartheid and settler colonialism, arguing that the displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements are part of a much wider process of territorial dispossession.
She has also challenged Israel’s international backers, accusing governments of providing diplomatic protection and military assistance while failing to uphold their obligations under international law.
In her July 2025 report, she went further still, naming companies including Microsoft, Amazon and Google, alongside arms manufacturers and financial institutions, which she said were helping to sustain Israel’s occupation and military campaign. She called on governments to sever trade and financial ties with Israel, impose an arms embargo and hold companies accountable.
On Friday, Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera: “The Costa Rican authorities’ decision to bar Francesca Albanese entry comes in the context of increasing efforts aimed at muzzling criticism of Israeli authorities’ atrocity crimes against Palestinians, ensuring impunity for these abuses, and other governments’ complicity in them.”
Who is Francesca Albanese?
Born to a lawyer and a homemaker in a small town in the Campania region of southern Italy in 1977, Albanese has said her interest in Israeli-Palestinian politics was shaped by her father’s library, where she encountered the writings of Holocaust survivor Primo Levi. She was also inspired by her older brother’s bedroom posters supporting Palestine during the first Intifada.
After studying law at the University of Pisa and human rights at SOAS in London, she pursued a career with the UN, first in Africa, then in Geneva and finally in Jerusalem with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, before going on to be appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories in May 2022.
Is this the first time Israel and its allies have targeted Albanese?
No.
Israel and its supporters have been campaigning against Albanese for years, repeatedly accusing her of anti-Semitism and anti-Israel bias and calling for her removal from her UN post.
The campaign intensified in 2023, when Israel and pro-Israel organisations stepped up demands for her dismissal following allegations that some of her public comments crossed the line into anti-Semitism.
In January that year, 11 US members of Congress signed a bipartisan letter urging the UN to remove her, while Israeli government officials also called for her resignation. Albanese rejected the accusations, saying they were intended to discredit her work documenting Israeli abuses.

Bruno Fernandes: Man Utd activate captain's 12-month option to extend contract which now ends in 2028
Bruno Fernandes' contract was expiring at the end of this season but it will now run until the summer of 2028; the Man Utd captain and the club are in agreement that it makes sense to return to negotiations in the future, with full focus on improving the club's current position
Friday 27 November 2026 14:18, UK
Manchester United have triggered their 12-month option to extend captain Bruno Fernandes' contract.
His deal was previously expiring at the end of this season but will now run until summer 2028.
United have been in talks with Fernandes over extending his contract since the summer.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Man Utd news & transfers🔴
- Man Utd fixtures & scores | FREE Man Utd highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
Sky Sports News understands both parties are in agreement that it makes sense to return to negotiations in the future - with full focus on improving the club's current position.
Triggering the club option now is logical from United's perspective, as clubs could have approached Fernandes over a pre-contract agreement in January. This contract clause activation prevents that.
Meanwhile, Fernandes was absent from United training on Friday - ahead of their game against Brentford on Saturday - due to illness.
Fernandes is understood to be under the weather and is being kept away from squad ahead of the Brentford game.
On whether he'll make the game, Mauricio Pochettino said: "We don't know. He got a virus in Portugal. He finished the game with a problem and today he cannot be part of the training session.
"We'll see. We are going to se during the day, and [Saturday], how he wakes up. We are not going to take any risks."
What Fernandes and Man Utd have said on contract talks
Last week, Fernandes exclusively told Sky Sports that United have offered him a new contract - but he has put discussions on hold as he insists the club's priority must be returning to winning ways.
Fernandes has rejected two contract offers from United. The club's initial proposal was made in the summer when discussions first began over a new deal, but was turned down by the Portuguese, who signed his last contract in August 2024.
The United captain said: "I've seen people saying that he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years. If I wanted more money, I wouldn't be here.
"I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.
"Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here. The thing is, I've always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it's time for me to move on, I will move on.
"I'm not going to be the player that I've seen many in this time at Manchester United. They're going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, 'Bruno, it's time to part ways', I'm going to be the first one walking out the door.
"Yeah, the club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay. And there are no negotiations going on. We spoke about the contract at the end of last season, we came in the beginning of this season speaking about the contract.
"But about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations because the most important thing now is that the club gets back to win games.
"My aim will always be to win the Premier League and the Champions League within the club I am."
Man Utd chief executive Omar Berrada also spoke to Sky Sports last week about Fernandes' contract talks and said: "Listen, I've said before, we have a tremendous amount of respect for Bruno. We're very fortunate to have him as a captain.
"What he's done for this team over the last six, seven years is absolutely incredible. Last year he won, I think, all the individual awards you can win.
"And we're very proud to have him as captain. It's true that we're having conversations about his new contract, but I prefer to keep that private. I think it's something that needs to be discussed behind the scenes between him and the club."

items.text:
Aside from dealing with my calendar, there’s one thing I want AI to do: tell me if I’m about to miss the bus.
Android’s DIY widgets are a bit of vibe-coding fun
You can have a good time brewing up widgets — as long as you don’t expect too much.
What I need is a widget. It needs to tell me real-time arrivals for the bus stop near my house. Tapping around on my phone screen to open the right app and select my stop will slow me down enough to miss a bus. I need glanceable information, and I hoped that Android’s vibe-coded widget feature could help me out here. It hasn’t, to my disappointment, but I still had a good time cooking up other widgets.
Google announced the ability to create custom widgets using AI back at I/O in the spring. It’s called Create My Widget, and it’s part of Android’s suite of “Gemini Intelligence” features. It’s in beta, and only just started rolling out to Pixel phones earlier this month. I was hyped. Not only does this feature raise tantalizing questions like “What is an app?” and “Where does the app live?” — stuff we live for here at The Verge dot com — it has potential to help me make my home screen ridiculous.
I fired it up on a Pixel 11 Pro and cooked up my first few widgets, including one that shows a different quote from Jurassic Park every hour — the original film, not any of the sequels, naturally. It took about 20 seconds to make, and it rules. Tapping the widget opens a thread in r/MovieQuotes, so there’s not much software magic going on under the hood, evidently. But did it bring me real joy to read the words “That is one big pile of shit,” on my home screen? It did.
I also made a widget that will display the words “Tut tut, looks like rain” whenever it’s raining. This is silly, and it accomplishes nothing except making me happy. I couldn’t think of anything clever it should say when there’s no rain, so it just says “No rain right now” otherwise. But I live in Seattle, so I’ll get a lot of mileage out of this widget.
The create-a-widget interface suggests a few ideas and categories, leaning on more practical uses like habit trackers and recipe inspiration. Fine, I’ll try something normal, I thought. I’m trying to get better about my daily mental health walk, so I had it make a widget for logging a week’s worth of walks. I was hoping for something visual that would trick my little monkey brain into keeping a streak going. Instead, I got something simply labeled “Log Walk” that triggers Gemini to add a walk to my calendar when I tap it. At least Gemini suggested the extra step of creating a checklist where I could mark off the days of the week as I completed my little walk.
It took me a minute to get my head around it, but many of the widgets are basically little prompt shortcuts for Gemini. You tap one, it pulls up the Gemini interface on your home screen, thinks for a while, then comes up with whatever you were asking for. The kinds of widgets you can make also seem to fit into some well-defined templates. You can create a widget that displays a countdown to a holiday or certain event on your calendar. You can show a recent score and upcoming game time for your favorite sports team. For anything more open ended, your widget will pull from Google search results (suggest a different three-ingredient cocktail recipe every day, for example) or prompt Gemini to figure it out for you. I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature. Fair, I guess.
I was hoping for mini apps I could customize to my liking, but this is more of a one-size-fits-all feature
That’s why my bus schedule widget didn’t really work out. I asked for a list of real-time arrivals; it gave me a tile that reads “Bus Arrivals” and uses Gemini to search for arrival times for the stop I specified. Gemini is helpful for some things but useless for this; it gives me a wordy response about how often the bus runs and when I might expect it to arrive based on the schedule. Not what I had in mind. On the bright side, my Jurassic Park quote widget had some words of wisdom for me: “Life, uh, finds a way.” That’ll do for now.

items.title: French and Bulgarian presidents condemn violence at Marseille v Levski Europa League game
items.summary:
The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome.
Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including
items.text:
The presidents of France and Bulgaria have condemned violence that broke out at a Europa League fixture between Marseille and Levski Sofia in the Stade Vélodrome.
Television footage showed Marseille fans cornering a group of Levski supporters in the stands before beating them relentlessly, including with a belt. One Levski fan is seen bleeding from the head as he receives multiple blows while trying to protect a female friend. Reports from inside the stadium on Thursday suggested violence began after a Levski supporter was seen making a Nazi salute.
The Marseille prosecutor’s office said it would open an investigation into the trouble, specifically accusations that French fans committed “aggravated intentional violence” against Levski supporters, and that it would also pursue allegations of “incitement to hatred after Nazi salutes and provocations from the Bulgarian fans”.
A statement on behalf of the French president, Emmanuel Macron, on Friday said he condemned the violence “in the strongest possible terms” and that it had “no place in sport or in public places”. He also insisted “these acts would not go unpunished”.
The Bulgarian president, Iliana Iotova, described the violence as “unacceptable” and “shocking” and said: “The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world. Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety.”
The country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said he had spoken to Macron about the incident which had resulted in 11 Bulgarian fans being hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilised Europe,” Radev said. “I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Another Europa League fixture on Thursday, between Besiktas and Hapoel Beer Sheva, was suspended for 30 minutes owing to fighting. Uefa’s account of the disruption that occurred at a neutral venue in Batumi, Georgia, said the game had been suspended to allow local police to subdue fighting between Besiktas supporters. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said some fans had been denied entry.
Turkey’s football federation strongly condemned what it described as “unacceptable” actions undertaken by Georgian police targeting Besiktas supporters who unfurled a pro-Palestine banner during the match.
A Uefa statement, however, said: “Uefa understands that the escalation between the local police and Besiktas’ supporters – which caused the temporary suspension of the match – started following an intervention of the local police in the sector of the Besiktas supporters to neutralise clashes that had erupted amongst Besiktas’ own supporters.”
Uefa condemned the violence at both matches and said it had appointed inspectors to conduct disciplinary investigations. “Uefa competitions are founded on the principles of respect, fair play, integrity and safety,” a statement said. “The events witnessed at the above-mentioned matches run counter to these fundamental values.” Any investigation would “examine all available evidence to establish the relevant facts and circumstances”, the statement said.
Last season Marseille were hit with a partial stadium closure after fans launched fireworks and pointed lasers into the field during a Champions League fixture against Atalanta.

Germany news: Parliament approves €556 billion 2027 budget
Published November 27, 2026last updated November 27, 2026
What you need to know
- German lawmakers to vote on 2027 federal budget
- Left Party hosts summit on femicide and violence against women
- BSW party conference starts in Dresden
- Rheinmetall lowers revenue forecasts
- Chancellor Merz to meet Pope Leo on Monday
Welcome to DW's coverage of what Germany is talking about on Friday, 27 November. Catch up on yesterday's news here.
German minister sticks to 'pension at 63' plans
German Labor Minister Alexander Schweitzer (SPD) submitted his draft pension reform legislation on Friday in which he reportedly intends to maintain the option of retiring two years early without benefit deductions for those with 45 years of pension contributions – a policy often referred to as the "pension at 63."
At the same time, however, eligibility requirements are set to become more stringent and more closely tied to an individual's actual lifetime work contribution.
In practical terms, this means that individuals with a long working life will still be able to retire two years early without deductions.
From 2029 onwards, however, only periods of employment, child-rearing, and the care of relatives will count toward the 45-year contribution requirement.
Periods during which an insured person received unemployment benefits, sickness benefits or transitional allowances – or held only a low-wage, part-time "mini-job" – will no longer be credited.
For weeks, Germany's coalition government partners, the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and Schweitzer's center-left Social Democrats have been struggling to reach a compromise on this issue.
A pension commission had proposed abolishing this popular type of pension, a proposal opposed by the SPD.
A group of leading coalition politicians, including Schweitzer, reportedly held final discussions regarding the plans as recently as Wednesday evening.
German parliament approves 2027 budget
Germany's ‌lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, voted in favor of a €556 billion ($610 ‌billion) 2027 ‌federal budget on ‌Friday, taking on additional debt to boost defense and infrastructure spending.
Total new borrowing will reach €210 billion, just short of the record €215.4 billion recorded in 2021 ‌during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to budget figures.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government has vowed a push to strengthen Germany's core civilian infrastructure and rebuild its military after decades of underinvestment.
"It is right that we invest in the railways and in climate protection," said Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil in parliament on Friday, defending his budget. "It is right... that we invest in our security."
German core defense spending will increase from €82 billion to almost €110 billion. When additional spending from the special defense fund is also taken into account, total defense spending will pass €150 billion.
"We are putting up the money for defense so that Ukraine can defend its freedom," Klingbeil said. "No child born in Germany today should ever have to experience war again."
But there was criticism of the budget from the opposition Left Party, with party leader Ines Schwerdtner accusing the government only ever talking about emergency and war.
"But for millions of people in this country, the emergency comes every month when money gets tight," she said. "But you're not interested in these emergencies."
317 members of parliament voted in favor of the budget and 260 against it. There were no abstentions.
Merz to meet Meloni and Pope Leo
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz will have a private audience with Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican on Monday before meeting Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Rome later, a government spokesman confirmed on Friday.
Merz, himself a Catholic, had a brief encounter with Pope Leo at the pontiff's inauguration in May 2025, but this will be the pair's first private meeting.
According to Politico, who first reported on the planned meeting earlier this week, officials expect the discussion to focus on "human dignity, artificial intelligence and efforts to bring peace to Ukraine."
Afterwards, Merz will be received with military honors by Italian Prime Minister Meloni, with whom he will hold talks on Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine, economic cooperation and, "with certainty," the European Union budget for the period 2028-2034, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF).
Negotiations over the MFF in Brussels this week ended without agreement, with Germany leading a group of more fiscally conservative member states which also includes Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Belgium and the Netherlands.
Italy, on the other hand, along with countries like Poland and Spain, would like to see a more ambitious EU budget.
Rheinmetall lowers medium-term revenue forecast
German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall has revised its medium-term revenue forecast for 2030 down from around €45 billion to between €33 billion and €37 billion, with an expected profit margin of around 20%.
The announcement, made on Friday at a market event in Hamburg, comes after the Düsseldorf-based company also lowered its forecast for the current year following delays in major orders notably from the German government.
In July, the German defense ministry canceled a multi-billion-euro contract to produce six new type-F126 naval frigates and there are now reportedly delays in an expected large-scale order of Boxer armored fighting vehicles (AFV).
Rheinmetall chief executive Armin Papperger said the government was negotiating hard on price and that he would only sign off on the deal once "sufficient profitability" was guaranteed.
Meanwhile, Rheinmetall is set to deliver 66 additional Lynx AFVs to Romania, part of an order which now totals 298 such vehicles.
The deliveries to the European Union and NATO member state are set to begin in 2028 and be completed by 2030.

items.text:
Why did Georgian police clash with Turkish football fans over Palestine?
Georgia’s Interior Ministry says 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured during clashes.
Police in Georgia have detained at least 16 people following clashes between football fans at a game between Turkish and Israeli clubs.
The Europa League fifth round match between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva was hosted in Georgia instead of Turkiye.
The coastal Georgian city of Batumi was selected last month as a neutral territory to host the game for “safety and security reasons” because of fears of protests over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, according to the European football association, UEFA.
Despite the precaution, tensions between fans spilled over into the stadium and the match was suspended for 30 minutes. Once play resumed, Besiktas won the game 2-1.
It is not the first time violent clashes have marred football matches involving Israeli clubs since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in October 2023.
Here’s what we know about the latest unrest:
What happened in Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva’s game?
Tensions between fans had already been rising before kickoff in Batumi on Thursday.
According to the Georgian news outlet Civil Georgia, videos on social media showed groups of Besiktas fans marching through Batumi and physical confrontations between fans and police officers.
Turkiye’s Anadolu Agency reported that the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel opposition.
In the 26th minute, the game was temporarily suspended when clashes broke out between Georgian police and Besiktas supporters. Turkish media outlets reported that police entered the stands and used pepper spray against Turkish fans.
According to reports, the police involvement came after a fan displayed a Palestinian flag and banner.
Turkiye’s TRT World reported that police surrounded the fan and used pepper spray, adding that video later showed a Besiktas fan being carried out on a stretcher and others being injured during the intervention.
What have Turkiye and Georgia said after Europa League match?
Omer Celik, spokesperson and deputy chairman of Turkiye’s ruling AK party, posted on X that the “intervention and violence” against the Besiktas fans who unfurled a ‘FREEDOM FOR PALESTINE’ banner and held a Palestine flag was “unacceptable”.
“Besiktas fans spoke on behalf of the alliance of humanity and became the voice of humanity. We strongly condemn the Israeli team’s provocations on the pitch. We extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to our fans who were injured in the incidents and taken to hospital. We are closely monitoring the condition of our citizens,” Celik said.
But Georgian Interior Minister Sulkhan Tamazashvili told reporters that UEFA officials confiscated the fans’ Palestine flags and Georgian state authorities played no role in the confiscation.
Tamazashvili said that 16 people were detained and three ministry employees injured.
“While marching from European Square towards Batumi Arena, some of the fans of the football club ‘Besiktas’ stood out by their aggressive actions,” the ministry said in a statement.
“They violated the public order by making indecent shouting and shooting of various objects, disobeyed the legal demands of the police, resisted law enforcement and physically confronted them.”
Police took appropriate measures to curb the violence, de-escalate incidents and ensure public safety, including the use of what it called “special means”, the ministry added.
It denied that the use of force was related to the display of pro-Palestine banners and flags.
“We categorically deny this information and emphasise that violent actions by fans and physical confrontation with law enforcers prior to the display of flags and banners have just begun while marching towards the stadium.”
How have Besiktas and other Turkish clubs responded?
Besiktas said it condemned the use of “disproportionate force”.
“We have initiated formal inquiries with our Consulate General in Batumi and with UEFA regarding the disproportionate force used by security personnel against our supporters; we will continue to monitor the situation closely until every single one of our supporters has returned home safely,” read a club statement.
In a post on X congratulating the Besiktas victory, the Turkish Football Federation said it would “closely monitor the unacceptable behaviour directed at our club, Besiktas and our supporters in Batumi tonight, and that we will take action with the relevant authorities to ensure that these incidents are fully investigated and the necessary steps are taken.”
Other Turkish Super Lig clubs, including Trabzonspor, Fenerbahce, Galatasaray, Erzurumspor, Basaksehir and Samsunspor, also condemned the use of force against Besiktas fans.
Why was Georgia hosting a UEFA match between Israeli and Turkish teams?
Since the onset of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza three years ago, Turkish clubs have not hosted Israeli opposition at home because of security concerns, with matches played in neutral territories instead.

items.text:
As Gambia gears up for election, can Barrow secure a third term?
November 27, 2026
Gambia votes on December 5 in a presidential election that takes place nearly 10 years after voters ended the 22-year rule of military ruler Yahya Jammeh.
President Adama Barrow, who succeeded Jammeh in 2017, is running for a third term despite an earlier pledge not to do so.
Barrow is running against the tiny West African country's main opposition leader Ousainou Darboe of the United Democratic Party, youth candidate Talib Ahmed Bensouda, who until last week was mayor of Kanifing Municipality, and four other candidates.
The field also includes independent candidates Almameh Gibba, a lawmaker who is backed by Jammeh, and former Vice President Isatou Touray, the only woman in the presidential race.
What matters to voters
Gambia is still governed under its 1997 constitution, which was adopted during Jammeh's rule.
A proposed replacement, which included presidential term limits, was rejected by the National Assembly in July 2025 after failing to secure the required three-quarter majority.
Barrow has defended his decision to seek a third term, saying voters should decide who leads the country. While he says he supports presidential term limits, he has argued that their introduction depends on securing enough parliamentary backing for a new constitution.
"I believe in term limits. And the Gambian people are the ones who elect a president," Barrow told reporters after submitting his nomination papers to the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) earlier in November. "So they decide the fate of a president and it is up to the Gambian people to decide whether I should be president for a third time or not."
Opposition parties have said their focus is not only on defeating Barrow but also on ensuring the election is conducted fairly.
Lamin Manneh, the United Democratic Party's administrative secretary, said the party's immediate priority is to ensure that the IEC conducts credible elections.
"The IEC has the responsibility of putting Gambians into confidence, ensuring that they guarantee us a credible election, a free election and a fair election," said Manneh.
Political analyst Malang Faye said the campaign was still taking shape after the official period began on November 16.
"The incumbent is already ahead," he told DW. "Some of the parties are yet to start their campaign." But he cautioned against judging electoral support by rally attendance alone.
"A large crowd at a political rally does not necessarily mean the same level of support at the ballot box," Faye added, noting that the election will test whether the democratic transition that began in 2016 can be consolidated.
Jobs, cost of living top of mind
Many voters say their immediate concerns are jobs, affordable living costs and better public services.
The World Bank has projected economic growth of 5.3% in 2026, but said extreme poverty is expected to remain at about 21%.
The 2025 Labour Force Survey puts youth unemployment at 11.5%, while 41.3% of young people are not in employment, education or training.
The figures reflect concerns voiced by many young Gambians about the lack of economic opportunities.
Alhagie Sama, a voter in Banjul, said young people need opportunities at home, rather than having to risk dangerous journeys abroad.
"We need a country where young people do not have to risk their lives crossing the Mediterranean Sea in search of opportunities," he said, adding that he wants the next government to deliver decent jobs, make basic necessities more affordable and improve access to health care and education.
Another voter and activist, Binta Bojang, said unemployment remains one of the country's biggest challenges.
"I would want the next president to prioritize employment, like particularly youth employment," she told DW, noting that joblessness goes beyond conventional definitions.
"We need to understand unemployment beyond the conventional definition, I mean the dictionary definition. Because unemployment definitely manifests differently in the lives of ordinary Gambians."
Election under observation
The Independent Electoral Commission has said 1,146,474 people are registered to vote. They will cast their ballots across 53 constituencies, 730 polling centers and 1,773 polling stations.
The commission has been training election officials in voting procedures, counting, verification and the transmission of results. It said the preparations are aimed at ensuring a peaceful and credible election.
International observers are also monitoring the process.
Following an invitation from Gambian authorities, the European Union has deployed an election observation mission, with teams of analysts and long-term observers across the country.
The United Nations has also urged candidates to honor the peace pact signed on November 16.
"History will judge not what you sign today, but what you do tomorrow and in the days to come," Barrie Freeman, the UN's deputy special representative for West Africa and the Sahel, told candidates.
Under the pact, presidential candidates pledged "to respect the independence and constitutional mandate of the IEC, to cooperate with it throughout the electoral process, and to seek redress through lawful and appropriate channels should disputes arise."
The December 5 election will test not only Barrow's bid for another term, but also whether the democratic gains made since 2016 can be translated into lasting reforms and improved living conditions.
DW correspondent Aminata Sanyang in Gambia contributed reporting.

items.text:
Has the reckoning with Serbia's pro-Vucic media machine begun?
November 27, 2026
"Beat them! Break their ribs," shouted the man in the studio during a live TV broadcast.
The man in question was Dragan J. Vucicevic, editor-in-chief of the channel Informer TV, and he was urging police officers to use force against demonstrators during a major student protest in June last year.
On November 25, Vucicevic was arrested by the police on suspicion of causing panic and disorder and obstructing justice. According to the authorities, his appearances "created an atmosphere of public lynching" and he labelled 97 citizens as enemies of the state.
The authorities cite instances where he described protesters as "scum," "hyenas" and "vultures" and spread claims that the students were preparing a "bloodbath" and a "civil war."
The prosecution says that between 2023 and 2026, Vucicevic systematically used Informer TV to conduct a campaign that incited hatred and targeted political opponents of the previous government, activists and independent journalists.
Who is Dragan J. Vucicevic?
Vucicevic's arrest comes at a time of profound political change in Serbia.
Following the Student List's victory in the parliamentary election in late October and the end of the Serbian Progressive Party's (SNS) 14-year rule, questions have arisen about the accountability of people who were part of the previous political and institutional system.
Critics have described Vucicevic as the mouthpiece of former President Aleksandar Vucic — a man who said publicly what the president was thinking but could not say himself because of the office he held.
"He [Vucicevic] is someone who stopped being a journalist a long time ago, and I think he crossed the line of being merely a propagandist some time ago. He was, in fact, a weapon in the hands of Aleksandar Vucic and his party," said Ivana Stevanovic of the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, a Belgrade-based organization named after a Serbian journalist who was killed in 1999 that provides media support and fights for press freedom.
Stevanovic told DW that Vucicevic used his media platforms to "target and endanger people, spread falsehoods that threatened their safety," all as part of a campaign against political opponents, journalists and media outlets who were critical of the government's record.
"This man showed a female student's intimate photographs live on air. He stalked people. He had his notorious 'Viewer Intelligence Service,' which secretly followed people and filmed them in their everyday lives, then turned that material into disgusting reports," she said.
"We had calls for violence, threats and insults against prosecutors who were doing their jobs and judges who were issuing lawful rulings, expressed in indescribable language. We had wiretapping, recordings of conversations in restaurants presented as conspiracies to overthrow the state. Media outlets and journalists were accused of plotting to assassinate the president, while their reporting was portrayed as treason and selling out Kosovo," she told DW, adding that "the entire television channel is one big criminal offence."
Court cases and compensation
The Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media (REM) has already issued several warnings and temporarily halted the broadcasting of certain programs on Informer TV.
Journalists' and media associations, civil society organizations and representatives of academia have launched an initiative to have the channel's broadcasting license revoked.
According to the Slavko Curuvija Foundation, more than 1,000 court cases concerning the protection of reputation and honor have been brought against Informer in recent years.
"Of the cases concluded over the past three years, courts upheld the claims in 92% of them," said Stevanovic. "Compensation was awarded to people whose rights had been violated. Informer even paid damages to the same individuals several times for the same lies, which it kept publishing about them. None of these financial penalties made them stop."
On one occasion, Dragan J. Vucicevic himself asked REM to impose a financial penalty on him rather than ban part of his program.
Money, it seems, was not a problem for Insajder Tim, the company behind all Informer media platforms (a daily tabloid newspaper, a television channel and an online portal).
Where did the money come from?
According to an investigation by Raskrikavanje, a fact-checking website that monitors the output of Serbian media, Insajder Tim, received around €273,000 ($299,000) in public funds in 2024 alone through public procurement contracts, advertising and media project funding.
Representatives of the Student List have claimed that the state-owned telecommunications company Telekom Srbija paid Informer between €500,000 and €700,000 a month.
Telekom Srbija, which also owns a cable network distributing television channels to millions of users in Serbia, cited business confidentiality when asked about the details of its cooperation with Informer.
SNS lawmakers protest
Vucicevic and his lawyers reject the accusations.
The defense argues that the proceedings amount to punishing someone for words they have spoken and raise questions about the boundary between freedom of expression and criminal liability.
Former President Aleksandar Vucic said Vucicevic had been arrested solely because of his journalistic work. SNS lawmakers walked out of a parliamentary session following news of the arrest and gathered outside the police station where the Informer editor was being held.
Stevanovic maintains that by arresting Vucicevic, Serbia is fulfilling its international obligations, including those arising from the European Convention on Human Rights and international conventions protecting civil and political rights.
"What constitutes a call for violence and a threat to democracy, security and health must be sanctioned and removed from the public sphere," she said.

items.text:
Duterte's ICC trial: What is at stake for the Philippines?
November 27, 2026
Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte will stand trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague on November 30, where he faces three counts of crimes against humanity linked to his bloody war on drugs.
For the families of the thousands killed during his anti-narcotics campaign, the trial is a chance for justice that has eluded them at home.
It is also a significant test of international justice at a time when the ICC faces increasing political pressure and questions about its ability to hold former heads of state accountable.
Yet, Duterte, 81, is still a popular figure in the Philippines, where many still regard his violent crackdown as one of his presidency's greatest achievements.
With his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte, a frontrunner for the 2028 presidential election, the proceedings in The Hague could become a defining issue in the Philippines' next presidential election.
Why is Duterte on trial?
Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016 following an expletive-laden, populist campaign in which he openly promised to kill criminals and drug dealers.
During his more than two decades as mayor of Davao City, he earned a reputation for transforming a notoriously violent city into a relatively safe one.
However, human rights groups found systematic extrajudicial killings by the so-called Davao Death Squad, which ICC prosecutors allege Duterte helped establish and oversee.
His disregard for political convention and promises of swift, uncompromising justice appealed to millions of Filipinos frustrated by corruption, crime and the perceived failures of successive governments.
"Filipinos who were deeply frustrated with everyday experiences of injustice and government inaction made them receptive to Duterte's promise of swift justice, even though extraordinary and violent means," Cleve Arguelles, a political scientist and CEO of Momentum Research, a pollster, told DW.
After assuming the presidency, Duterte extended his Davao law enforcement model nationwide. Police launched sweeping anti-narcotics operations, primarily targeting impoverished urban communities, while suspected drug users and dealers were also killed by unidentified gunmen.
A 'way of governing'
Philippine authorities officially recorded 6,252 deaths during anti-drug operations, with police claiming to have acted in self-defence. Human rights organizations estimate the actual death toll at between 12,000 and 30,000.
"Duterte's ruthless war on drugs was not simply a campaign against crime; it was a way of governing through killing," David Johnson, a professor of sociology at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, told DW.
"The extraordinary violence he ordered and encouraged was sustained by a combination of extraordinary problems of impunity in the Philippine criminal justice system and deep failures of democracy in that country,” Johnson said.
"These conditions made extrajudicial killing politically useful even though it was ineffective as crime control," he added.
Duterte also used state power to intimidate and suppress wide sections of Philippine society, including opposition politicians, civil society groups, journalists, lawyers and judges, Diane Desierto, a professor of law and global affairs at the University of Notre Dame, told DW.
Former president remains popular
The deterioration of human rights under Duterte damaged the Philippines' international standing and strained relations with its traditional Western partners, particularly the United States under President Barack Obama and the European Union, which threatened to withdraw Manila's preferential trade privilege.
Duterte left office in June 2022 as one of the most popular presidents in recent Philippine history. A survey conducted by pollster Social Weather Stations found that 88% of Filipinos were satisfied with his performance.
His daughter was overwhelmingly elected vice president in May 2022, while their allies dominated that year's Senate elections.
"Up to now, the Dutertes remain popular not in spite of the drug war but because of it,” Arguelles said.
Why was Duterte arrested?
Despite years of domestic and international scrutiny, Duterte remained at liberty for nearly three years after leaving office.
The ICC opened a preliminary examination into the drug war in 2018, prompting Duterte to withdraw the Philippines from the court's founding treaty. A formal investigation began in September 2021.
For much of his early presidency, President Ferdinand Marcos refused to cooperate with the ICC investigation.
What changed was the breakdown of relations between the Marcoses and the Dutertes, two of the country's most powerful political dynasties.
Marcos' father had ruled the Philippines as a dictator until he was overthrown in the 1986 People Power Revolution.
The alliance that brought Marcos Jr. and Sara Duterte to power in 2022 unravelled spectacularly after November 2024, when the vice president claimed she had arranged for Marcos to be assassinated in the event of her own killing. She has since faced successive impeachment efforts.
Philippine authorities arrested Rodrigo Duterte in March 2025, acting on an ICC arrest warrant issued four days earlier.
In April this year, ICC judges confirmed three charges of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder.
The trial will begin with opening statements, followed by testimony from prosecution witnesses. The process is expected to be extensive, potentially running until 2028, the year of the next Philippine presidential elections.
What does the trial mean for Philippine politics?
The Philippines is effectively confronting two different questions about the Duterte legacy: whether Rodrigo Duterte should be held criminally accountable for his presidency and whether his family should be entrusted with political power again, Arguelles said.

Jamie Overton took a career-best 5-12 as England thrashed Australia by seven wickets in the third T20 int
items.text:
England’s Overton takes 5-12 as Australia bowled out for record low in T20
Australia are bowled out for 108 as Jamie Overton claims career-best figures in England’s seven-wicket win in Brisbane.
Jamie Overton took a career-best 5-12 as England thrashed Australia by seven wickets in the third T20 international in Brisbane on Friday.
Overton’s figures were the best by an Englishman against Australia in T20s as the home side were bundled out for 108, their lowest score on Australian soil.
“I thought Jamie Overton was outstanding tonight,” England captain Harry Brook said.
“He’s worked hard and put in some extra graft at training.
“He simplified his game and reaped the rewards tonight – he had it on a string and it felt like we could change the field and make them make a mistake.”
Brook won the toss and sent Australia in to bat, and off-spinner Liam Dawson struck early when he had Australian skipper Mitch Marsh caught at mid-on.
Jake Fraser-McGurk and Sam Harper attacked during the powerplay, taking the score to 55 after five overs.
Harper raced to 26 off 14 balls before Dawson grabbed his second when the Australian wicketkeeper got a top edge to Overton at mid-on.
Overton then swung into action with the ball, claiming the next five wickets as Australia slumped from 65-2 to 92-7 and then collapsed to 108 all out when Sam Curran clean-bowled Billy Stanlake.
Aneurin Donald, who smashed 85 off 32 on the Gold Coast on Tuesday, got the run chase off to a spectacular start, belting 31 from just 11 balls.
But a rain delay seemed to help the Australians, as Brook holed out for nine after play resumed, before Donald fell for 32, leaving England 49-3.
Another rain break threatened to stop England’s momentum again, but Jordan Cox blasted 33 in quick time to give the visitors an easy win and go ahead in the five-game series 2-1.
Marsh conceded that Australia were outplayed by a better team.
“No excuses, we’ve got to be better,” he said.
“We’ve all played Big Bash games here (at the Gabba).
“You have to give yourself the chance to cash in at the back end (of the innings), but we didn’t get near that tonight.”
The two teams head to Sydney for the fourth game on Sunday night.

In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship
items.text:
Risks of child marriage in Iran complicated by war
November 27, 2026
For a girl still at school, marriage can mean leaving her education behind, becoming pregnant before adulthood and growing dependent on her family and husband.
In Iran, rights advocates warn that war and mounting financial hardship could expose more girls to those risks.
The warning comes as the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage is observed on November 27. The day was established during the UN General Assembly last year.
Although there is no evidence linking child marriages to the war, cases illustrate the danger faced by girls married as children, often with limited means of escaping abuse. Gaps in Iran's marriage statistics also make it difficult to measure the conflict's impact.
In one case cited by the Iranian human rights news agency HRANA, a 14-year-old girl in Kerman province who had recently given birth was reportedly killed by her husband.
Skylar Thompson, deputy director of Human Rights Activists in Iran (HRA), said she had reportedly been forced to marry at 13.
"While these cases cannot be directly attributed to the war, there are substantial grounds for concern that deteriorating socioeconomic conditions are placing more girls at risk," Thompson told DW.
What the figures show
Iran Open Data's analysis of the Civil Registration Organization's statistical yearbook identified 14,039 registered marriages involving girls under 15 in year measured roughly from March 2025 to March 2026. They accounted for just over 3% of all registered marriages.
The figure excludes girls aged 15 to 17. UNICEF defines child marriage as a formal marriage or informal union involving someone under 18.
Thompson said 31,646 marriages involving girls under 15 were registered in 2020–2021, indicating a longer-term decline in recorded cases.
But the latest figures largely predate the war, which began on February 28, 2026.
"The absence of recent, disaggregated statistics, coupled with the prevalence of unregistered marriages, makes it difficult to determine whether child marriage has increased since the outbreak of the war," she said.
When marriage becomes an economic calculation
The conflict has intensified pressures that can contribute to child marriage: lost income, difficulty staying in school and girls' financial dependence on their families.
In its October assessment, the World Bank described damage to infrastructure, disrupted trade and declining purchasing power, forecasting a 7.7% economic contraction in 2026/27.
Thompson told DW that families facing severe hardship may see marriage as a way to reduce household expenses, transfer financial responsibility or secure their daughters' future. Government backed marriage loans can also create financial incentives for some disadvantaged families to arrange marriages involving minors, she added.
Hossein Raeesi, a lawyer and adjunct professor in Carleton University's Department of Law and Legal Studies in Canada, described a similar risk.
When families cannot meet a girl's living costs, and education or other prospects are unavailable, they may push her towards marriage or force her into it, he told DW, while acknowledging that statistics on changes in numbers of child marriages since the war are still unavailable.
War and displacement
Displacement can further weaken children's access to education and protection. On March 12, the UN refugee agency estimated that up to 3.2 million people had been temporarily displaced within Iran, based on preliminary assessments. That was an early-war estimate, rather than a current displacement figure.
Thompson said displacement and disrupted schooling could isolate girls from teachers, social workers and others who might recognize pressure to marry and intervene
Financial dependence, limited independent legal assistance and insufficient shelters can leave girls with few alternatives, particularly when those arranging a marriage are also their legal guardians.
Few legal safeguards against child marriage
Article 1041 of Iran's Civil Code allows girls under 13 and boys under 15 to marry with guardian consent and court approval. Iranian law therefore provides no blanket prohibition on marriage below 18.
"Although Iranian law formally recognizes consent as a condition of marriage, it provides inadequate practical safeguards against familial coercion," Thompson told DW.
Raeesi said preventing a marriage was insufficient if a girl remained under pressure at home. Leaving home could also expose her to further danger without safe accommodation and practical support.
The concerns also extend to the online space. An HRA investigation published in October reported that the government-licensed matchmaking platform Adam and Eve displayed girls aged 13 to 17 as prospective spouses. Those findings do not establish how many marriages resulted or whether the war increased them.
What can be done to protect girls?
Raeesi called for a minimum marriage age of 18 for both sexes, alongside preventive intervention, financial assistance, education and safe accommodation.
"Education alone is not enough," he told DW. Families also need the means to support their children.
Thompson urged targeted financial assistance, measures to keep girls in school, confidential reporting channels and independent legal support. Safe accommodation must be accessible without permission from guardians who may themselves be responsible for coercion, she said.
According to rights advocates, effective protection means that a girl under pressure to marry can say no without losing her home, her safety or her chance to continue school.

items.text:
Philippines: VP Duterte says father's ICC case 'not a fair trial'
November 27, 2026
The Vice President of the Philippines, Sara Duterte, criticized the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Thursday, saying it would not provide a fair trial for her ex-president father's crimes against humanity case.
She said the court would try to "make a statement."
Former President Rodrigo Duterte has been detained at The Hague since his arrest on an ICC warrant in March 2025, over extra-judicial killings that took place between 2011 and 2019.
What is expected at Duterte's trial?
The trial begins on Monday, where Rodrigo Duterte is expected to plead not guilty. Witnesses will be called up to testify the next day, with more than 500 alleged victims represented in court.
"I think the ICC, after the ganging up of superpowers, (will) want to make a statement that they are in the right. So there is no-one else there that they would like to make a statement to. And that's the case of Rodrigo Duterte," said his daughter Sara.
Duterte said "China, Russia and our BFF the United States," all considered the ICC a "political organization" and not an impartial arbiter.
BFF stands for "best friend forever" and was likely a swipe at the Philippines' close ties with the US under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
Why is Rodrigo Duterte at the ICC?
Prosecutors at the ICC accuse the 81-year-old former president of funding and arming execution squads that murdered as many as 30,000 people.
He has been charged with three counts of crimes against humanity involving murder and attempted murder between 2011 and 2018.
Duterte is the first Asian former leader and only ‌the second former national ruler to appear before the court for crimes allegedly committed while in power. The other one was Laurent Gbagbo of Ivory Coast, who was ultimately acquitted in 2019.
Supporters of the former president, who was arrested in Manila, say he was "kidnapped" and sent to The Hague after his daughter had a bitter falling-out with current president Ferdinand Marcos Jr., with whom she had held an alliance that helped him win a landslide 2022 election victory.
Duterte: ICC trial is politically motivated
The younger Duterte is also facing an ongoing impeachment trial in the Philippine Senate and if found guilty, she would be barred permanently from elected office.
She said both her case and her father's ICC trial were related to efforts to make her ineligible to run for the 2028 presidential election.
"I still believe that it's about the 2028 elections, whether there will be elections or there will be no elections. It's about the change of leadership, if there will ever be a change of leadership," she told reporters.

items.text:
Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan?
US president’s new tariff regime targets China hardest, just weeks before Trump and Xi meet again at the G20 in Miami.
In February 2025, US President Donald Trump marked his return to office by kick-starting a trade war with China.
New tariffs, amid accusations that China was failing to prevent the flow of drugs into the United States, set the stage for an escalating economic confrontation between the world’s two largest economies, which stands to reshape global trade.
While Trump’s new trade tariffs regime hit allies and rivals alike, China took the fight head-on.
Washington first put a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods, citing fentanyl and immigration concerns, and Beijing responded by curbing exports of five rare earth metals key to defence, clean energy and tech products.
Then it came to a showdown with Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs in April, including 34 percent for Chinese products. A tit-for-tat exercise ensued as headline US tariffs on China climbed to 145 percent, while US goods entering China were slapped with tariffs of 125 percent, alongside restrictions on rare earth exports.
The tariff war seesawed for much of that year before the two leaders sat at a table in October, on the sidelines of the 2025 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in South Korea, to call a truce.
The limited-time pause in hostilities paved the way for a diplomatic thaw.
Trump then travelled to Beijing last May for talks with Xi, who then visited Washington in September for the first time in more than a decade. Trump embraced the Chinese president when he arrived in Shenzhen, China’s technology hub, earlier this month for this year’s APEC summit.
But then Trump returned to Washington and, in less than a week, his administration had announced a new tariff regime – its second attempt at reshaping its trade war after the Supreme Court declared his Liberation Day tariffs of April last year illegal.
“The practical purpose is simple: rebuild [the] tariff leverage the Supreme Court stripped away and force Beijing to the table before the next summit,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, the chief economist for Asia Pacific at investment bank Natixis.
‘Purpose changed somewhat’
This time, the Trump administration has announced plans to impose new tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods through unfair government subsidies, policies and suppressed wages.
China is subject to the highest rates – a new 20 percent levy that is still within the bounds of the trade truce that is set to expire in January. Washington has, however, threatened a 40 percent levy if trade talks break down.
Instead of the emergency powers it used the first time – and which the Supreme Court struck down – the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, alleging that targeted countries are making use of “structural excess capacity”. It has identified these 14 specific economies during an investigation it launched in March, but views China as the biggest offender, particularly in its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, a trade policy think tank in Singapore, said the “original intention” of the investigation “was to provide a more durable way to get back to the tariff levels” announced on Liberation Day.
“Over that time, I think the purpose changed somewhat,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Originally a means to apply tariffs, it seems clear that the White House wants a more sweeping use of Section 301, which allows a broad range of activities to be subject to possible negotiations and future punishment like tariffs,” she added.
Elms argued that Trump’s announcement coming in “now is rather interesting”, given he is due to meet with Xi next month, in Miami, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit. “This announcement adds another layer of possible tensions,” she said.
‘Right to retaliate’
Just before Trump landed in Shenzhen, where he was greeted by Xi on the tarmac, earlier this month, the Chinese leader had opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.
Xi also portrayed Beijing as a stable trade partner in contrast with the US, where Trump’s tariff war had already rattled global economic equations.
Responding to the latest round of tariffs this week, Beijing warned that it “reserves the right” to retaliate with steeper tariffs.
“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said, adding that Beijing “will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.
Referring to the eight-month investigation into “structural excess capacity” practices undertaken by Jamieson Greer, Trump’s trade representative, China said it was “a typical act of unilateralism that severely disrupts the international economic order and seriously violates WTO rules”.
Under the latest measures, Washington is seeking to take its economic confrontation with Beijing beyond bilateral trade, targeting the industrial policies of countries emerging as alternative manufacturing hubs but whose supply chains remain closely intertwined with China’s.
Hinrich Foundation’s Elms told Al Jazeera that while Beijing “is probably ok with a 20 percent tariff, they are undoubtedly less comfortable with the attempt to hold all other trade partners accountable to the US for engagement with China”.
‘China can blunt this’
Investment bank Natixis’s Herrero said that Trump’s latest tariffs “are less a grand strategy than a familiar negotiating ploy: keep the pressure on after a friendly photo-op”, referring to the meeting in Shenzhen.

items.title: Germany's tiny BSW is a party in crisis as it is set to hand the far-right AfD power in Saxony-Anhalt

items.text:
The BSW is set to play a major role in German politics once more
November 27, 2026
This fledgling party has experienced many highs and lows in quick succession. Launched in January 2024, it was named the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) to capitalize on the high profile and momentum of its founder, a former communist who had just exited the socialist Left party.
Since October 2026, the acronym BSW has instead stood for theAlliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason. In the past 34 months the newcomer party celebrated election successes at the European Parliament level and in German state elections. In the eastern states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party even took part in governing coalitions; however, both of these collapsed relatively quickly.
Even more painful for the BSW was its defeat in the general election in February 2025. The party failed to gain the 5% share of votes required to enter parliament, by less than 10,000 votes. With that, it was denied the country's most important political stage and took the matter to court, demanding a complete recount.
'Germany has the election scrutiny process of a banana republic'
But Germany's Constitutional Court dismissed the BSW's election challenge as inadmissible, pointing to a lack of evidence. "Simply insinuating the possibility of voting errors or expressing an unproven assumption does not meet the requirements for claiming an electoral mistake," the court explained. The court's decision was published about a week before the party's federal conference is due to be held in Dresden, the capital of the eastern state of Saxony.
"Germany's election scrutiny process resembles that of a 'banana republic'," was the angry reaction of former party leader Sahra Wagenknecht, who stepped back from frontline leadership of her eponymous party in December 2025. Since then, she has led its commission on fundamental values.
One of her successors at the top of the BSW is European Parliament lawmaker Fabio De Masi. In his view, the decision of the Constitutional Court was a "black day for democracy in Germany." Fellow co-leader Amira Mohamed Ali did not want to accept the rejected recount. "It remains unclear whether the Bundestag is correctly composed and whether the approximately 2.5 million BSW voters have unjustly been deprived of their parliamentary representation," she said.
The disappointment at the failure to enter the Bundestag runs deep. The party has not recovered from this setback. It again failed to win representation in 4 out of 5 state parliaments in elections this year, albeit narrowly.
In Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate, as well as in the city-state of Hamburg in 2025, the BSW received less than 2%. This clearly shows that it is politically irrelevant in the western German states.
Will the BSW help the AfD to power in Saxony-Anhalt?
They find themselves in the spotlight, however, because of the role they are set to play in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the BSW got 5.3% of the vote in September.
Despite being the smallest party in that state parliament, they are set to play a pivotal role. They are the only political party that has indicated a readiness to help the election winner, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) into power.
The AfD, which is classified as right-wing extremist in Saxony-Anhalt by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, won the election with almost 44% of the vote. Although his party does not hold an absolute majority in parliament, lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund wants to be voted Germany's first-ever AfD state premier in December.
The BSW has not indicated any intention to vote for Siegmund, but if he falls short of winning the absolute majority of 42 votes in the first two rounds of voting, a third round will be held in which a simple majority will suffice to win. The BSW has announced plans to abstain from that vote. Siegmund would then only need to pick up one more "yes" vote or abstention.
During the secret ballot for the state parliament speaker, AfD candidate Tobias Rausch received 9 votes more than his party has lawmakers. It is not known exactly who they came from. Alongside the AfD and BSW, there are 4 other parties in the state parliament: the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), environmentalist Greens, socialist Left Party and center-left Social Democrats (SPD).
Sahra Wagenknecht rejects a firewall against the AfD
The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will be at the center of the party's upcoming conference in Dresden, because the BSW's increasing closeness with the far-right party is highly controversial.
Several BSW members, including board member Christian Leye, criticized this path in a column published in the weekly magazine Die Zeit. They recalled their party's founding consensus: "The clear political demarcation from the AfD." They quoted party founder Sahra Wagenknecht, who at that time said: "Of course we will not collude with the AfD."
"We are starting a party so that all the people who are considering or have voted for the AfD out of anger or disappointment — but not because they are right wing — have a credible political home," she continued.
Wagenknecht has long argued that the so-called "firewall" policy of mainstream parties refusing to work with the AfD has failed. This is also why she is rejecting the idea of entering a mathematically possible governing coalition with the other parties in Saxony-Anhalt. "We are basically agreed that we neither want to go into coalition with the AfD, nor tolerate them, just as much as we do not want to participate in a firewall coalition," she told German news agency dpa.
How the BSW plans to make its way through this dilemma at its party conference is totally unclear. Fabio De Masi, who replaced Wagenknecht as co-chair in December 2025, seems well aware of this. He told German media network RND that dealing with the AfD continued to be like "riding on the edge of a razor blade."
This article was originally written in Germ

items.text:
Ukraine's Heraskevych hails EU pushback against Russian athletes
November 27, 2026
Ukrainian skeleton racer Vladyslav Heraskevych has welcomed a move by the European Union to take a tougher stance on Russian athletes competing in the 27-member bloc.
Heraskevych is one of the most outspoken critics of Russia's reintegration into international sport. He made headlines at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan-Cortina when he was disqualified for his helmet honoring Ukrainian athletes killed in the war with Russia.
On Monday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed banning Russian athletes from competing under their own flag at sports competitions within the European Union (EU) and urged member states to consider denying visas in such cases.
"Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities," von der Leyen said.
In an interview with DW, Heraskevych described the EU move as coming "better late than never."
"We waited a long time for this backlash," he said at the World Cup event in Altenberg, his first competition since the Winter Olympics.
"I'm really happy to see that people start to care about sports and they understand the value of sports as a huge platform."
Europe pushes back
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) paved the way for Russia's full return to international sport by ending its recommendation that Russian athletes be allowed to compete as neutrals, without their flag, colors or anthems. The IOC also said Russian teams should be allowed to return to international competition.
Several major Olympic sports, such as swimming and gymnastics, have already fully reinstated Russia, despite the country's ongoing attacks on Ukraine.
"It makes no sense to me," Heraskevych said.
However, in recent weeks, there has been a growing European pushback against the easing of Russia's sporting isolation.
Among the catalysts was a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) to overturn a ban on Russia in international ice hockey. That prompted seven European countries to say they would refuse to play against Russia, while Germany, at one point, said withdrawing as host of next year's Men's World Championship was an option.
Putin wades into dispute
The dispute over the CAS ruling drew a response from the Kremlin.
"It is a flagrant violation of the Olympic Charter [the IOC's rulebook] and leads towards the destruction of Olympism as a whole," Russian President Vladimir Putin said in China last week.
"Sport, like art, should bring people together."
Meanwhile, a group of Nordic and Baltic countries want the EU to go even further, pushing for an immediate EU-wide visa ban on all Russian athletes.
"The matter is too urgent to wait until [new visa rules] enter into force," the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and Sweden wrote in a November 23 letter to von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa.
"From my perspective, the IOC is in a very big crisis," Heraskevych said, referencing the European pushback. Blanket bans could have a huge effect on Los Angeles Olympic qualifying events in Europe.
Can sport be separated from politics?
Under its president Kirsty Coventry, the IOC has sought to bring Russia, an Olympic powerhouse, back in from the cold. Coventry has argued that athletes shouldn't be punished for the actions of their governments, and the IOC has strengthened its political neutrality rules in the Olympic Charter.
However, Heraskevych takes exception to the idea that sport should be kept out of politics.
"We are not living in a bubble," he said.
"Already more than 800 people who were part of the sport family in Ukraine were killed. Ukrainian hockey stadiums, Ukrainian swimming pools, anything related to sports have also been attacked. So we cannot separate sport and politics in Ukraine. The same way Russian sport is involved in politics."
Citics have accused Coventry of cosying up to Russia. In September, it emerged that she had written a letter to Mikhail Degtyarev, Russia's sports minister and president of the Russian Olympic Committee, wishing him luck ahead of an international sports forum.
Degtyarev has been sanctioned by the EU. The IOC has declined to comment on the letter but not denied its existence.
Heraskevych said he was not "angry" with any particular Russian athlete, and even floated the idea of a team of Russian refugees.
"I am not against peaceful athletes competing," he said.
"They should be part of competition only if they are part of a refugee team. So, if they have refugee status in another country, and if they condemn the war that Russia started in Ukraine."
