George Russell says Lewis Hamilton is a 'ruthless competitor' like Max Verstappen but has 'incredible grace and values'
George Russell's long-standing feud with Max Verstappen reignited at the Las Vegas GP after the pair collided in final practice; watch Russell's full exclusive interview during Sky
items.text:
George Russell says Lewis Hamilton is a 'ruthless competitor' like Max Verstappen but has 'incredible grace and values'
George Russell's long-standing feud with Max Verstappen reignited at the Las Vegas GP after the pair collided in final practice; watch Russell's full exclusive interview during Sky Sports F1's live coverage of the Qatar Grand Prix from 2.30pm on Sunday
Friday 27 November 2026 13:08, UK
George Russell says Lewis Hamilton is an equally "ruthless competitor" to Max Verstappen but that his former team-mate has "incredible values, grace and dignity".
Russell and Verstappen's rivalry reignited last weekend at the Las Vegas Grand Prix following a minor collision between the pair in practice, after which the Mercedes driver publicly criticised his Red Bull rival's conduct.
Verstappen won a thrilling race in Las Vegas that saw Russell challenge him for the lead for long periods before crashing and finishing ninth, and afterwards the four-time world champion said the Brit is "so far below my level" before adding that it was "fantastic" seeing him make an error.
- Qatar GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports
- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column
- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺
Speaking exclusively to Martin Brundle during an interview that will air during Sky Sports F1's live coverage of the Qatar Grand Prix on Sunday, Russell said he found Verstappen's verbal attack on him "amusing", before drawing a comparison between the Dutchman and seven-time world champion Hamilton.
"He [Verstappen] is a ruthless competitor and I massively respect that, but there's also Lewis Hamilton, who I've spent three years team-mates with and watched my whole life," Russell said.
"And obviously Toto [Wolff, Mercedes' team principal] spent 12 years with [Hamilton], who is equally a ruthless competitor and absolute animal behind the wheel, but obviously has incredible values and grace and dignity.
"And Lewis is somebody who I really look up to and who is an incredible role model for young kids coming through.
"But there is no right or wrong, there's just opinions. Everyone has different opinions, and some people like driver A and some people like driver B, and as I've grown older, I don't really let it affect me as much."
'I know where Toto stands on Verstappen off the record'
Wolff has previously tried to sign Verstappen from Red Bull with Russell telling Sky Sports F1 in June 2025 that his own contract extension was being delayed by Mercedes' attempts to recruit Verstappen.
Wolff was photographed holidaying with Verstappen, has rarely criticised the Dutchman in recent years. and in Las Vegas called the back and forth between the two drivers a "good factor of the entertainment" in Formula 1.
Asked about Wolff's position on his clashes with Verstappen, Russell said: "Well I know where he [Wolff] stands off the record, so I won't probably repeat that.
"Toto and I were flying back after the race in Vegas and we did have quite a laugh about the comments that were said after the race.
"But we just know how certain people go about their business."
Russell: Verstappen comments would have affected me more a few years ago
Verstappen and Russell have clashed several times since the latter joined Mercedes in 2022, a move that made battles between the pair for top positions a more regular occurrence.
Their first collision came in the Sprint at the 2023 Azerbaijan Grand Prix on the opening lap, before their rivalry spectacularly ignited at the end of 2024 when Verstappen was given a one-place grid penalty for impeding Russell at the 2024 Qatar Grand Prix.
Verstappen said Russell's conduct with the stewards in Qatar meant he had "lost all respect" for the Brit, who then responded with a remarkable explosive verbal attack on the Dutchman the following week at the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix.
Russell said at the time that Verstappen had threatened to put him "in the wall" in Qatar, and said that "people have been bullied by Max for years". Verstappen questioned the accuracy of Russell's claims and labelled him a "loser" and "backstabber".
Reflecting on his comments during the 2024 meeting with the stewards in Qatar, Russell said: "Well, I wasn't trying to let him off. I mean, I didn't go in there saying, 'that's fine'."
On the alleged threat that the Mercedes driver said followed in Abu Dhabi, Russell added: "That's how he [Verstappen] goes about his business. I've known him long enough that I know, again, that was a bit more of a laugh away comment, I thought."
The pair came collided at the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix after Verstappen felt Russell forced him wide and effectively retaliated by making contact with Russell and was given a 10-second time penalty for the incident.
Russell downplayed suggestions that the feud had begun during the pair's karting days, before insisting he hasn't let Verstappen's latest comments overly affect him.
"We actually didn't have that many comings together in karting," Russell said. "He's a year older than me so we only raced together once in 2011, and then obviously he fast-tracked his career.
"I found it all quite amusing afterwards. But obviously he won the race, I had a c**p race, and he's able to have the last laugh, so I'm sure he quite enjoyed that. A few years ago, it probably would have affected me a lot more, but we're different characters.
"I respect his driving talents immensely and everything he achieves on track. Obviously, maybe off track we do things slightly differently, but that's how it is."

items.text:
European football violence causes concern with far-right claim in UEFA game
Claims of Nazi salutes at UEFA Europa League game in Marseille headline night of further violence in European football.
Violent clashes at two European football matches have stoked concerns about fan violence and prompted the leaders of France and Bulgaria to condemn behaviour that had “no place in civilized Europe”.
Images showed masked and bloodied fans wielding improvised weapons and metal pipes during a brawl at a UEFA Europa League match on Wednesday evening between Marseille and Levski Sofia, which the Bulgarian club said began when their fans were attacked by supporters of the French side.
A photographer working for the Reuters news agency said the clashes at the Stade Velodrome in Marseille had started after a supporter from the visitors’ stand made a Nazi salute.
Clashes also broke out at a Europa League match in the Georgian city of Batumi between Turkiye’s Besiktas and Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva, forcing the referee to suspend the match for 30 minutes.
European football’s governing body UEFA told Reuters its disciplinary body “would assess the match reports before considering any potential ‌next steps”.
What was the reaction to the Marseille and Levski Sofia game?
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he and French President Emmanuel Macron spoke by phone and condemned the violence at the Marseille-Levski Sofia match, in which Marseille police said 11 Bulgarian fans were hurt, five of whom were taken to hospital.
“We share the position that aggression and violence have no place in civilized Europe,” Radev said on Facebook.
“I thank President Macron for his personal commitment to this case, for the medical care provided to the injured by the French authorities, for the measures taken to ensure the safety of Bulgarian citizens, and for the perpetrators to be held accountable.”
Macron said he had condemned “with the utmost force” acts of violence targeting Bulgarian fans, which he said had “no place in sport or in public space”, and told Radev they would not go unpunished.
A protest was planned in front of the French embassy in Sofia later on Friday.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said: “Violence, racial hatred and provocation have no place in our stadiums.”
Manuel Bompard, a French lawmaker for the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party in the Marseille department, commented on a video on social media appearing to show a Levski fan performing a Nazi salute.
“Congrats to the Marseille fans who responded with an antifascist chant,” Bompard wrote on X. “The far-right has no place in our stadiums!”
Batons fly, flares lit in Marseille and Levski Sofia clash
Levski Sofia, which lost the match 1-0, said masked fans had attacked its supporters with batons and flares. Some had let off flares and tried to get through the barrier as security staff tried to hold them back.
Images showed fans attacking each other through a netted fence separating sections of the stadium.
Before Thursday’s match, French authorities had introduced a sevenfold reduction of ticket sales to Levski supporters and imposed additional restrictions on their movement to and around the stadium, aiming to curb risks of violence.
The Bulgarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it would request a thorough investigation. Marseille said it would conduct its own analysis and was working closely with law enforcement.
What happened in the Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva match?
The match between Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva had been moved from Istanbul for what UEFA said were safety and security reasons.
Clashes in the stands led referee Morten Krogh to suspend the match in the 26th minute, and it resumed after a 30-minute delay. Georgian police entered the stands, and television footage showed one ‌fan being carried out on a stretcher.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that police used pepper spray. Besiktas condemned what it called “disproportionate force” by security staff and said a number of fans had been denied entry. Besiktas went on to win 2-1.
Turkish Football Federation chair Ibrahim Haciosmanoglu defended the ‌decision ‌to keep Israeli clubs out of Turkiye following Israel’s invasion of Gaza in 2023 after the deadly Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel.

items.text:
How East Germany boosted Vietnam's coffee industry
November 27, 2026
Coffee lovers, brace yourselves: Imagine taking your first sip, expecting the rich aroma of roasted coffee beans, only to discover that your cup contains a concoction made from ingredients you can barely identify.
That's exactly what millions of outraged East Germans experienced in 1977. But what led to this?
Foreign currency deficit versus soaring prices
A poor harvest in Brazil saw global coffee prices skyrocketing, creating a major problem for East Germany. Unlike West Germany's Deutsche Mark, the East German Mark was a domestic currency with no value abroad.
Even under normal circumstances, the country constantly struggled to obtain the hard currency it needed to pay for imports. In 1974 and 1975, East Germany spent around 150 million Valutamarks — the term used in East Germany for the West German Deutsche Mark — on imported coffee. The following year, it had to pay almost five times as much.
However, this rate of inflation could not be passed on to consumers because, "In the GDR, there was the dogma of stable prices — set by the state through law," explains historian Stefan Wolle, a consultant at the DDR Museum in Berlin. "Prices were set by the Politburo, not by businesses. And they weren't allowed to change. What sounds wonderfully socially minded at first glance had serious negative economic consequences, because production costs were far higher than retail prices."
The government needed a solution. On August 1, 1977, it introduced "Kaffee Mix" as a substitute for popular coffee brands back then such as Kosta, Rondo and Mocca Fix. The fine print on the packaging promised "a blend of select green coffee beans and carefully balanced coffee substitutes."
In plain English, that meant 51% of the blend consisted of imported coffee beans. The rest was a mixture of rye and barley, along with chicory and either spelt or sugar beet. It tasted disgusting, Wolle recalls.
Even the coffee machines appeared to reject the concoction. The mixture expanded and clogged the filters in cafeterias and restaurants. Some machines were even said to have exploded.
'Pure rat poison'
Public discontent boiled over during this "coffee crisis." People responded by boycotting the product and with biting sarcasm. "The difference between a neutron bomb and coffee mix: There isn't one — the cup stays intact, but the person is destroyed.." A sharper dig? "It's pure rat poison."
More than 14,000 complaint letters poured into government offices. On September 1, the Ministry for State Security, better known as the Stasi, reported to the leadership of the ruling Socialist Unity Party of Germany or SED, that Kaffee Mix was being "rejected by broad sections of the population." (Editor's note: The SED was the only ruling party in East Germany then).
To understand the intensity of the backlash, it's important to recognize coffee's special place in East German society. "Coffee was, in a way, the social glue that held together East Germany's particular brand of conviviality and camaraderie," says Wolle. During the 1960s and 1970s, people would gather for coffee after lunch, often accompanied by homemade cakes or treats from the bakery. "It was a sacred hour in every workplace and office. It was a huge mistake for the SED leadership to slaughter this sacred cow, so to speak."
Care packages from relatives in the West
According to Wolle, real coffee was still occasionally available in the larger cities. But in smaller towns and rural areas, people often had no choice but to make do with Kaffee Mix. East Germans who had relatives or friends in West Germany and regularly received packages from them could count themselves lucky. "Our relatives and friends in the West knew what was in short supply in East Germany, so they would usually include a big bag of good West German coffee," Wolle recalls.
It is estimated that around 25% of all coffee consumed in East Germany came from the West. During the height of the coffee crisis, that share was briefly even higher. "Of course, the SED leadership had mixed feelings about people receiving so many packages from the West," Wolle says. "Police officers and full-time party officials weren't allowed to have contacts in the West. But ordinary citizens didn't care." Especially after the blend stirred up such negative reactions.
Trading weapons for coffee
East Germany's leaders responded by looking to their socialist allies in Africa for help. They negotiated special agreements with Angola and Ethiopia. "Instead of paying in hard currency, they paid with military equipment — weapons and trucks," Wolle explains. "Weapons that were used in Ethiopia's civil war."
But the East German leadership sought a long-term solution, and eventually established a partnership with another socialist ally: Vietnam. "Coffee had already been grown there under French colonial rule," says Wolle. "People knew that coffee grew well there and that the quality was good."
Coffee from Vietnam: Too late for East Germany
Starting in the 1980s, East Germany invested heavily in developing the infrastructure needed for large-scale coffee cultivation in Vietnam, Wolle explains. It supplied machinery and equipment, built transportation routes, and provided housing for plantation workers. "There was just one catch: Coffee plants take several years before they can be harvested."
By the time the plants were finally ready to produce coffee, the Berlin Wall had fallen and East Germany was a thing of the past. "But the Vietnamese benefited enormously," says Wolle. "They converted the plantations into private enterprises fairly quickly." Today, Vietnam is one of the world's largest coffee exporters. "What's surprising is that most people don't even know that."

items.text:
Saudi strike kills ’11 civilians’ in Yemen’s Taiz: Houthi media
Hostilities between Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi-backed coalition continue to push Yemen into a humanitarian crisis.
Saudi air strikes have killed 11 civilians in Yemen’s Taiz governorate, according to news media affiliated with the Houthi armed group.
The attack reported on Friday hit the city of al-Turbah, located south of the provincial capital, Taiz.
The alleged strike comes as hostilities in Yemen continue between the Iran-backed rebel Houthi group and government forces backed by Saudi Arabia.
A local source said that a residential building was struck and that “most” of the victims were children, according to the media report.
Rescue teams retrieved eight bodies from the site, the report said. Three people remain missing beneath the rubble.
Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports. The Saudi Arabia-led coalition supporting the internationally-recognised Yemen government did not immediately comment.
The coalition said later on Friday that it had destroyed a drone launched by the Houthis toward Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region.
Humanitarian crisis
Yemen has been racked by violence since the Iran-backed Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, and other parts of the country in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to lead a military coalition in support of the internationally recognised government in March 2015.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and the Houthis resumed in July, as the United States’ war on Iran escalated hostilities and the collapse of a 2022 ceasefire.
Some 13,343 people have been killed or injured since August, according to the World Health Organization, while the country is sliding into a humanitarian crisis.
The Food and Agriculture Organization and the World Food Programme said on Friday that Yemen is among conflict hotspots that face severe food insecurity.
The Norwegian Refugee Council warned this week that the renewed fighting has displaced thousands and piled pressure onto dangerously underfunded aid efforts.
Aid from the US, Germany and others has shrunk considerably in recent years, the nongovernmental organisation noted, saying it has received only 12 percent of funding for emergency shelter support in Yemen so far this year.
“Fighting has again displaced entire communities, while disrupted supply routes have driven up food and fuel prices,” NRC Secretary-General Jan Egeland said, warning that families across Yemen are being pushed deeper into need.
“All parties to the conflict bear responsibility for the vast scale of harm here,” Egeland stated.
Calling for better humanitarian access and civilian protection, he demanded that “the powerful countries backing the armed actors must commit to making this a reality”.

items.text:
It was a vidiprinter moment worthy of a double take. Ross County 1 Cove Rangers 1 (Keir 52). Would Cove, scrapping for survival in Scottish League One, put an unlikely end last Saturday to the most emphatic run in British senior football? Don’t be silly, retorted County; four goals in the closing 17 minutes extended the Dingwall side’s goal difference to plus 45 (for 56, against 11). Played 16, won 14, drawn two. There is as much chance of Mike McCarthy settling down for Christmas dinner with Aaron Rodgers as County missing out on promotion back to Scotland’s second tier. Taking in cup competitions they have scored 102 goals this season.
Assessment from the captain, Brian Graham, of a frankly irrelevant loss on penalties to Stenhousemuir in the Challenge Cup epitomises the County approach. “We should have been five- or six-nil up at half-time,” an irked Graham says. “That shows the standards we have set. We lost a dubious goal, which shouldn’t have stood.” Earlier in that competition County whacked 14 past a Hearts youth side before defeating a Celtic B team including two Chelsea loanees and a £3m midfielder.
Unsurprisingly there is cynicism, laced with jealousy, about County’s position. They are portrayed as wild spenders in a frugal environment. A club in the wrong competitive domain. The analysis does not stack up. Graham, the scorer of 21 goals across all competitions, is 39. The prominent Adam Emslie was last on loan at Cove after being rejected by Aberdeen. Luke McCarvel arrived via Kelty Hearts and Cumbernauld Colts. Lewis Reid is previously of Stranraer, Lewis Strapp a signing from Airdrie. County have a batch of Scottish Championship-capable players, not Premiership-ready ones. Their form is still extraordinary.
“People don’t know the ins and outs of this club,” says Graham. “I speak to the chief executive – as the captain I need to work on the bonuses – and I can see a massive difference now to what it was previously. There’s not players on wages like the exaggeration of what people say they are on. People just play guessing games. But look at Scottish football as a whole; budgets do not give you the right to win matches anyway. It’s players on the pitch who have to do it.
“If you had said to me I would have 21 goals in November, I would have laughed at you. I had a number in my black book which I have exceeded. I now have another number in there.” Not that wider records – 100 goals, 100 points or an unbeaten league campaign – are viewed similarly. “We haven’t spoken about that,” Graham says. “We are getting a lot of plaudits, a lot of people speaking about it, but the manager insists we keep our feet on the ground and don’t listen to outside noise. When you put yourself in the position we have, teams are desperate to beat us.”
Only Boreham Wood, with 16 wins and three draws from 19 National League games and 53 goals scored, are in touching distance of County’s win percentage. Graham is ideally placed to speak on County’s journey. Now in spell three, he played for them in the top flight and when Hibernian were vanquished in the League Cup final of 2016. A club who had been a small Highland League team in the early 1990s were giving bloody noses to the big boys. Subsequent years brought trauma, culminating in successive demotions from 2025. County kept faith in the summer with their manager, Stuart Kettlewell. Graham returned to spearhead a fightback. Pre-season games, which began in late June, included a comprehensive closed-doors win over Aberdeen.
“The manager had to build a new squad and bring in younger players,” Graham says. “The manager has created a new culture that he spoke to me about before I came in. We had to get back to basics, everybody wanting to train every day and fight for their jersey. He has created that environment; nobody is resting on their laurels and everyone is pulling their weight. The manager and coaching staff have really high standards, which the players know about. Nobody gets away with any nonsense.”
The emphasis on attitude is apposite. County have a generous owner and, owing to geographical location, were always known to pay decent salaries to prise players from the central belt. In recent times, received wisdom was that players were using the club for a payday that came free from accountability. The team spiralled as a result, having previously brought wider attention on Dingwall and boosted the local economy.
“It is a community club, a family club,” says Graham. “We have excellent volunteers. One woman comes in every week with her spaniel – I think the dog likes the pies – to help clean the stands but she is not the only one. You want to come to your work because there are good people here.
“At the start of the season the fans were a bit dejected, the numbers weren’t quite there. Slowly but surely people are coming back to support us, they realise this is a team to get behind. It’s a real Ross County side, people willing to fight for the jersey, which is what this club is all about.”
On Saturday County host Brora Rangers in the Scottish Cup. While not quite a derby – the towns are almost 50 miles apart – this is a compelling fixture. Brora look capable of leaping from the Highland League to the Scottish League, as County did in 1994. Graham wants a cup run to bring finance into a business which has had to withstand sharp income drops. There is a more endearing cause. Bobby Wilson, who presided over County’s league entry having scaled European highs when a player with Dundee, died on 18 November. A celebration of Wilson’s life will soon take place at County’s home. He would approve of this resurgence.

items.text:
Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
Thanksgiving Storm Aftermath, Black Friday Economy, Eisenkot's Coalition Talks
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Today's top stories
Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.
- 🎧 Flooding caused most of the damage and disruptions, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Several bridges in New Jersey were shut down, and people were seen kayaking through usually busy streets in parts of coastal Virginia. Exceptionally high tides, known as the King Tides, have been battering the West Coast. Lonsdorf says there's still a lot of work to do before roads return to normal, but there is some hope. The storms should move out and the tides should recede heading into Saturday, as people begin their journeys home.
Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.
- 🎧 NPR's Alina Selyukh says surveys indicate people are cutting back on other spending to spend during the holiday season. She notes that while gas and housing costs have been big drivers of inflation, the prices of goods, including gifts, have not risen as dramatically. She also says she's watching a shift in the trend of how people are shopping. Although most people are doing their holiday shopping online, more are choosing to shop in person.
The Trump administration has banned asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and canceled thousands of pending asylum applications over the past nearly two years. Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.
Behind the story
This essay was written by Stephan Bisaha, NPR's personal finance correspondent
I was at a book club recently, chatting with a small group, when someone from another circle asked what we were discussing. Driven by an instinct to instigate (perhaps a side effect of our earlier heated book talk), I said the "benefits of AI."
After some anti-AI sighs, I told them about a source whose AI agent saved him $50 without him even asking. A friend uses Claude for her retirement funding decisions. Others are turning to AI for holiday shopping.
New AI agents can now help buy gifts, from brainstorming to checkout. Would I trust AI with my own shopping? Apparently not.
Those cheap acoustic panels AI recommended? Only a good deal if I ignored how tiny they were. The griddle it suggested? Too big. Then I started worrying about how much of my personal data my AI assistant was collecting and eventually asked it to forget everything about me.
Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer guided me through another attempt for my book club's gift exchange.
I gave Meta's new AI agent, Muse, my requirements: a $25 cap for a Gen Z crowd and something that makes noise, per the organizer's request (way to stereotype the radio reporter).
Muse's suggestions? A karaoke mic and a plastic, yodeling pickle. I wasn't sold on either.
Once again, my shopping cart is empty.
My next attempt with AI, though, might not be this holiday season. Instead I'm planning to buy a Tamagotchi for the gift exchange. Remember those virtual keychain pets from the '90s? A throwback to a time when you could take your digital companion shopping without worrying about your privacy.
Weekend picks
Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:
🍿 Movies: The holiday season is packed full of can't-miss films. These are 17 movies that you should see before the year ends.
📺 TV: Parks and Recreation star Amy Poehler and creator Michael Schur reunite for Dig, an ensemble comedy about a team of archaeologists caught up in a series of mysterious events after uncovering an ancient artifact in Greece.
📚 Books: Why settle for one book recommendation when you can get more than 300? Now's the time to browse this year's Books We Love.
🎵 Music: NPR Music's Stephen Thompson and Lars Gotrich join host All Songs Considered Robin Hilton to attempt to build a canon of music for giving thanks, spending time with loved ones and, of course, celebrating food. Check out their playlist here.
🍴 Food: A few years ago, Israeli American chef Alon Shaya spearheaded the Rescue Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, exploring food's role in World War II. He has compiled his stories and dishes in a new cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.
3 things to know before you go
- Rocker the coonhound has won best in show at this year's National Dog Show. His glossy coat and big, floppy ears bested six other dogs that each won top honors in their groups.
- When Dungeons & Dragons came on the scene 50 years ago, some parents complained it kept their kids holed up inside. These days, the once-nerdy pastime is a screen-free parent's dream.
- Bakers across the country have taken inspiration from Little Free Libraries to offer free sweet treats to their neighbors.
This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

items.text:
McInnes tempers 'anxiety' as Rangers seek top spot
- Published
Derek McInnes says Rangers should not experience any anxiety about the prospect of going top of the Scottish Premiership as the Ibrox side look to extend their four-match winning run.
Rangers host in-form Falkirk on Saturday (15:00 GMT), who have won six on the bounce in the league, and victory would move McInnes' team top before leaders Celtic travel to face Hearts on Sunday.
"I don't think there should be anxiety when you're trying to go top of the league at all," McInnes said.
"Obviously, you want to be top of the league come the end of the season.
"If you've got an opportunity to go there, it's important you try and take it."
Ryan Naderi netted an early second-half equaliser then set up Djeidi Gassama as Rangers turned a 1-0 deficit into a 3-1 lead before Aberdeen scored a consolation in Tuesday's Premiership match at Ibrox.
It was Naderi's 11th goal of the season and McInnes spoke of his awareness of the now Czech Republic international last season while managing Hearts, who have used a data analytics firm for much of their recent recruitment.
"Last January, obviously, when we first saw that Rangers were linked with Naderi, like everything else, I would say to [Hearts sporting director] Graeme Jones, 'how do they rate him?'
"Because you're always curious, it's just the way it is. It's brilliant when you see other teams round about you signing a player that's not rated!
"He was someone that I think was well known to them. Brugge had an interest in Ryan, I think, and I think USG potentially had an interest in him as well but the kind of money, the fee, it just went away from them.
"The feeling was that he could help Rangers and make them better.
"I had a good conversation with Ryan when I first came in the door and what we felt this season could look like for him.
"He's stood up brilliantly to the injuries to Youssef [Chermiti] and Lawrence [Shankland] and he's had to be the guy. He's led the line brilliantly and I love the goals he scores. All top strikers have intelligence to be in the right place at the right time."
And the manager reiterated his stance about keeping hold of assets like Naderi through January.
"These conversations that I have with Jim [Gillespie, chief executive] on a regular basis about players that we should be speaking to and trying to address and secure and give them a wee bit more security and a wee bit more comfort for us, these conversations, I think, have been ongoing," McInnes said.
"The club's well aware of what needs to be done and what we shouldn't be doing and Ryan's been part of that conversation."
McInnes' side won 2-1 away to Falkirk in September but the Bairns held Danny Rohl's Rangers to a 0-0 draw at Ibrox last season.
"What they have got is a bit more physicality," McInnes said of the Bairns.
"They can play when they want to play so they've mixed it up a bit this season, I think, and been a wee bit more pragmatic maybe at times as well, but they've still had those results that's got them where they are in the league and we've got a difficult game ahead of ourselves."

Iran has openly claimed its strikes on Gulf states throughout the war. So why is it denying an attack on Kuwait?

items.text:
Italians killed in Kuwait: Why is Iran denying responsibility?
Iran has openly claimed its strikes on Gulf states throughout the war. So why is it denying an attack on Kuwait?
Two Italian technicians have been killed in a drone attack on a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, the first European civilians to die amid the United States-Israel war on Iran.
Kuwait and Italy have both blamed Iran. Tehran, which has for the most part not denied, outright, strikes on US military assets hosted by its Gulf neighbours and described those attacks as self-defence, has this time denied any role and has suggested the strike was a “false-flag” operation.
The denial has raised two questions: Who was behind the attack and, if it was Iran, why is it not taking responsibility?
Here’s what we know:
What happened in Kuwait?
On Thursday, several drones targeted military installations in Kuwait, according to Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani.
Kuwait’s army initially described the target only as a “vital site”. Tajani later told the Italian Senate that it included an air-defence detection station where two technicians from Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defence company, were working.
The men were named by Italian media as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, from Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, from Rome. They were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system used by Kuwait’s armed forces.
They were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured.
The two dead men are the first European civilians to be killed as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran since it began in late February. A French soldier was killed in a drone attack in Iraq in March.
This was the first fatal strike on Kuwait in several months, although the country has been one of the hardest-hit Gulf states during the war. Its oil facilities, power infrastructure and airport have all been targeted at various points in the conflict. An Indian traveller was killed and 63 people were injured when drones hit Kuwait international airport on June 3 .
Iran said it last struck Kuwait on November 18 .
What have Kuwait and Italy said about the latest incident?
Both countries have blamed Iran for Thursday’s drone strike.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry condemned what it called a “sinful” attack and said the country reserved its right to take all measures to protect its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents.
After a call between Kuwait’s foreign minister and Tajani, the Kuwaiti ministry said the two had jointly condemned the strike.
Tajani told the Italian parliament the drones were “of Iranian origin”. The Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, Jasem Albudaiwi, also condemned what he called a “brutal attack”.
What has Iran said?
Iran has denied any involvement.
“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.
Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. As of Thursday evening, Kuwait had not publicly commented on the call with Araghchi.
Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, speaking for both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, said Iranian forces had conducted “no military or offensive operations whatsoever” in the region. He called the attack a “false flag” operation, while a military statement accused the US and Israel of using it as cover for continued aggression.
The Iranian embassy in Rome said it “categorically rejects the allegation”, suggesting the attack could have been staged to drag Europe into the Iran war.
The denial stands out because Iran has rarely disowned its attacks since US-Israeli strikes began in February. In November alone, it issued five statements claiming strikes on neighbouring states, four of them on Bahrain and Kuwait.
Tehran usually tries to justify those strikes as self-defence, arguing that it targets US bases from which Iran is attacked, not the countries that host them.
This is not the first time Iran has denied an attack on Kuwait, however. When a power and desalination plant was hit on March 30 , killing an Indian worker, Iran also claimed that Israel was responsible.
What do we know about who launched the drones?
Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of Middle East studies at the University of Tehran, said Iran’s record of claiming its strikes should be taken seriously.
“Whenever the Iranians do something, they announce it,” he told Al Jazeera. “This time, as on three or four occasions during the war, they said, ‘This wasn’t us.'”
He argued that Iran would have little reason to hide this attack. “They’ve struck the Americans,” he said. “Would they be afraid to announce they’d hit Italians?”
Ahmadian said other parties in the region, such as Israel, might want to “complicate the situation” by blaming Iran, which he called “the ready-made party to blame”. He added that some in Iran also suspect Ukraine, which he argued has been trying to raise its strategic value to Washington.
As the US ran down its stock of expensive Patriot missile interceptor systems against a barrage of cheap, mass-produced Iranian Shahed drones, Ukraine offered its expertise to the US in March on how to combat the drones, which are also used by Russia.
Ahmadian said US involvement could not be ruled out either. Iran has previously told regional governments that the US was behind strikes on two sites during the war, he said.
“We’re looking at someone fishing in troubled waters. Otherwise, if it were the Iranians, they would have announced it,” he added.
Paolo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and a professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University in Washington, dismissed the idea of US involvement.

items.summary:
French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two
items.text:
French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.
Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.
Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.
Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.
The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.
The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.
A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning
With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.
He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."
But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.
On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.
"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.
Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").
The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.
"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.
Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate
The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.
Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."
The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.
In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.
Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.
His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

Russia’s hybrid war on Europe continues to evolve, but has failed in its objective to deter support for Ukraine,
items.text:
Russia’s hybrid war on Europe evolving, but failing: IISS
Growing sabotage and cyberattacks have damaged European infrastructure, but have not reduced support for Ukraine, analysis says.
Russia’s hybrid war on Europe continues to evolve, but has failed in its objective to deter support for Ukraine, according to analysts.
Moscow has been increasing its use of unconventional warfare in the past year or so, employing sabotage, reconnaissance and intimidation, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report published on Thursday.
Moscow has rejected accusations from Western governments and intelligence services that it is waging a Europe-wide campaign to disrupt support for Kyiv.
Incidents have included a drone attack on a German airport, arson and other attacks on energy infrastructure and defence manufacturers, and persistent airspace and border incursions.
Sabotage ‌attacks on European infrastructure rose by 16 percent in the 12 months leading up to September 2026, the IISS said. The use of arson and explosives roughly doubled.
“Targeting of critical infrastructure (specifically military-industrial and transport) accounted for more than half of recorded incidents between October 2025 and September 2026,” the IISS said.
The “attacks have damaged European critical infrastructure (ECI) and raised the costs of protection”, it noted.
Attacks are also becoming more sophisticated, according to the report.
“Unskilled recruits still carry out most operations. But a semi-skilled tier now uses more complex methods, including improvised explosive devices with timed and remote detonators,” the report reads.
Russian intelligence services remain a threat to European security, the IISS said, but noted that European support for Ukraine in its nearly five-year defence against Russia’s invasion has not been deterred.
“Russia’s unconventional war on Europe has so far failed in its strategic purpose,” with military assistance to Ukraine from Western allies continuing to increase, the report said.
IISS data shows that European defence spending grew by 12.6 percent in real terms in 2025, matching the rate of 2024, while Russia’s rose by 3 percent.
NATO has expanded surveillance of the Baltic Sea and its eastern airspace, while the European Union has launched a Preparedness Union Strategy.
Germany and Poland, the main conduits for military support for Ukraine, have suffered the most incidents. IISS predicts they will remain the main targets.
On Tuesday, Britain warned defence companies working with Ukraine’s military that they faced an increased sabotage threat.
Russia’s embassy in London retorted that “Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the UK.”

items.text:
Old wounds reopen as Kyrgyzstan’s Osh embraces a new urban project
Redevelopment reshapes the city, but some worry as residents are displaced and cultural heritage appears at risk.
Osh, Kyrgyzstan – Kyrgyzstan’s second-largest city is in the throes of a major regeneration programme.
New IT hubs are planned for Osh, as well as apartments, schools and nurseries. Transport projects, a waste-to-energy plant and a livestock complex are being worked on too. A “modern school” for 530 children, kitted out with solar panels, was completed in 10 months and will open in the coming days, the government announced last week.
But several hundred homes have been demolished to make way for new infrastructure, stirring fears about the future and the character of the old city.
The fast-paced campaign to modernise could also affect Osh’s mountain of Sulaiman-Too – a UNESCO World Heritage site.
Osh lies just 5km from the border with Uzbekistan and is home to about 470,000 people – about 40 percent are Uzbek.
Kyrgyz authorities in the town “want to erase us from the history of this city”, said 84-year-old Mogamed Kambarow, an Uzbek with a white beard and sun-bronzed face. In March, about a third of his home was destroyed as municipal authorities worked to widen Alisher Navoi Street.
“They sent bulldozers, pulled down the walls and left,” said Kambarow, who was at home at the time. He received no compensation and lives in the remaining parts.
Neighbours alerted each other when the demolition began. An 11-year-old girl was injured by falling bricks and taken to hospital, he said.
Kambarow’s memories haunt him. He was around when violence engulfed the city before.
In 2010, inter-communal tensions spilled over into violence. More than 400 people were killed and thousands of homes were destroyed. Most of the victims were ethnic Uzbeks.
In 1990, shortly before the collapse of the Soviet Union, as Uzbeks demanded more autonomy and as land disputes raged, fighting and riots broke out between the two groups and hundreds were killed.
‘It isn’t only Uzbek property that is damaged’
But Gulgaky Mamasalieva, head of the International Centre Interbilim, an organisation in Osh that provides legal help to residents today, says the current redevelopment affects everyone.
“It isn’t only Uzbek property that is damaged,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that more than 750 households were affected by the latest demolitions, including many Kyrgyz families.
According to a report by Interbilim, 65 percent of households first learned that their homes were going to be demolished when city workers painted the Russian word snos, meaning “demolition”, on their walls.
Some residents received letters telling them to leave within three days. Others, like those on Navoi Street, were visited by the mayor, who announced the plans himself.
“But people expected that there would be some paperwork done first,” said Mamasalieva.
Osh sits at the eastern end of the Ferghana Valley, the agricultural heart of Central Asia. The area is divided between three former Soviet republics: Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.
Historically, the city was predominantly Uzbek, but when the borders of the Soviet republics were drawn up in 1924-27, Moscow gave it to the Kyrgyz.
In those days, the whole city used to look like the quarters along Navoi Street, where flat-roofed houses hide behind high fences and yards full of grapevines offer some shade from the scorching sun. These areas are known as “mahallas” – an old word for an administrative and community unit.
As the years passed, a university was established, factories built, and the population grew.
Just behind Kambarow’s house, a path leads up Sulaiman-Too. The mountain is a holy site for Muslims and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.
It is believed that the ancient Greek geographer Ptolemy mentioned the mountain in his book Geography. Babur, who was born in the Ferghana Valley and later founded the Mughal Empire, built a house of prayer on its summit.
The building was destroyed during a Soviet campaign against religion in the 1960s, but rebuilt in the late 1980s. Some Muslims believe that visiting Sulaiman-Too three times is equal to making one pilgrimage to Mecca.
There are also three cemeteries on the mountain where old gravestones rise from the long grass.
Retired pilot Abduraim Amanbaev, 73, climbs Sulaiman-Too every Friday, after prayers. He takes a shortcut through the cemetery to avoid paying the entrance fee, as the mountain is also a tourist attraction.
“The oldest grave dates back to the 14th century,” Amanbaev said.
His family home has been destroyed three times during his lifetime. The first time was in the 1960s, when the Soviet authorities modernised the city. The second was in 2010, during the ethnic violence. Now, it is happening again. “People are tired,” he said. Half of his house was destroyed. He lives in the other half and has not been compensated.
Mamasalieva from Interbilim told Al Jazeera that the city was supposed to agree on compensation with each household before demolishing their property. Disputes should have gone to court. While they received guarantee papers signed electronically by the vice-mayor, the documents did not detail compensation packages, she said.
Only families whose houses were completely destroyed were offered new flats. More than 100 households were moved to Ene-Say, a residential area 10km (6 miles) outside Osh. Another 64 families were given flats in an apartment block in the city.
But for some, relocation has caused further problems.
“We still haven’t been given the deeds for this flat,” said a 37-year-old woman who now lives in Ene-Say, who requested anonymity.
Without official ownership, her family cannot register their new address or access free healthcare and other services. Some families said they have also been asked to pay the government the difference between the value of their old homes and their new flats.

items.title: What Spain’s election means for Morocco
items.summary:
What Spain’s election means for Morocco
The vote could reshape diplomatic relations, but shared strategic interests will continue to bind the two countries.
Spain’s November 29 general election comes at a difficult moment both domestically and internationally. The snap election was triggered by an i
items.text:
What Spain’s election means for Morocco
The vote could reshape diplomatic relations, but shared strategic interests will continue to bind the two countries.
Spain’s November 29 general election comes at a difficult moment both domestically and internationally. The snap election was triggered by an internal political crisis after parliament voted down the government’s housing decrees including stronger protections for tenants, with one of the ruling coalition’s members going against the proposals.
Foreign policy crises have also cast a shadow over the election, significantly influencing the substance of the campaign and potentially its outcome. Of particular importance are Spain’s relations with Morocco, which involve several sensitive and overlapping issues, notably the status of Ceuta and Melilla, irregular migration and the question of Western Sahara. These have placed Morocco at the heart of Spain’s political and electoral debate in recent months.
A poll conducted by Cluster17 showed that relations with Morocco and the situation in Ceuta and Melilla topped the list of international issues likely to influence how Spaniards vote, with 34 percent of respondents selecting them. Relations with the United States came a distant second at 9 percent, followed by the conflict in the Middle East at 8 percent and the war in Ukraine at 4 percent.
The positions Spanish political parties have adopted towards Morocco during the election campaign range from moderate to confrontational. While incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who remains in office until the election, has taken a restrained and cautious approach towards Morocco, parties such as Vox have adopted a more hardline stance, going so far as to promise a review of Spain’s relations with its southern neighbour.
A distinction must be drawn, however, between the electoral promises parties make in the media, sometimes in an attempt to outbid their political rivals and how they actually exercise power.
Political parties may adopt more hardline positions while in opposition or on the campaign trail, but once in government, they become responsible for managing the affairs of the state, rather than merely pursuing their party agendas.
This often prompts them to adopt more pragmatic approaches, particularly on foreign policy issues of strategic importance. Moreover, on certain issues, such as Western Sahara, existing state commitments limit the parties’ room for manoeuvre and require a degree of caution. Regional and international balances of power also remain important factors in shaping foreign policy.
Between electoral rhetoric and enduring interests
To understand Spain’s political and electoral debate over Morocco and its implications for relations between the two countries, it is necessary to distinguish between three categories of issues on which their interests intersect and sometimes conflict: immediate concerns, medium-term interests and long-term strategic issues.
This distinction helps separate crises arising from short-term political developments from structural disagreements that transcend changes in government and the balance of power between political parties.
The first category encompasses immediate issues and short-term political tensions. These are closely intertwined with Spain’s domestic political landscape, both shaping and being shaped by the balance of power within parliament and government. The 2002 crisis over Perejil Island and the migration crisis in Ceuta in the summer of 2026 offer two contrasting examples.
The former occurred under the Popular Party government led by Jose Maria Aznar and developed into a political and military confrontation. Relations gradually returned to normal following an agreement to restore the status quo, brokered by then-US Secretary of State Colin Powell.
The 2026 crisis, meanwhile, occurred under a left-wing coalition government, which largely succeeded in containing it. Although the episode was described in Spain as the most tragic mass border crossing in the country’s history, with some 72,000 migrants crossing the border in a single week, the government was able to manage the crisis but could not escape its domestic political repercussions.
From this perspective, some of the current electoral rhetoric towards Morocco can be understood as a reflection of domestic political competition rather than a new strategic direction. Hardline positions on Ceuta and Melilla, migration and relations with Rabat should be viewed in the context of the competition for votes, bearing in mind the distinction between electoral promises and the feasibility of translating them into government policy.
The second category concerns the shared economic, security and political interests that form the backbone of Moroccan-Spanish relations. These include trade and investment, cooperation on energy, migration and border control, and efforts to combat terrorism and organised crime.
The importance of this category lies in the practical and immediate nature of these interests, which would be difficult for any Spanish government, regardless of its political affiliation, to ignore or sacrifice.
Although these interests are sometimes affected by short-term political tensions, they require both countries to exercise a degree of pragmatism and caution in managing their differences. They are therefore among the most important factors in containing crises and ensuring the continuity of bilateral cooperation.
The third category encompasses long-term strategic and structural issues dictated by geography and history, which are not necessarily determined by the political orientation of successive governments.
Foremost among these are the status of Ceuta and Melilla and the other islands Morocco seeks to reclaim and the question of Western Sahara. They also include the countries’ perceptions of one another, shaped by history, collective memory and political discourse, which have influenced how each views the other and understands it

- Published
A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor
items.text:
Ex-Kenyan governor jailed for 25 years over pregnant girlfriend's murder
- Published
A former Kenyan governor has been jailed for 25 years for the murder of a university student who was seven months pregnant with his child.
The High Court on Friday sentenced Zacharia Okoth Obado, the former governor of Migori County, alongside two former aides over the 2018 killing of Sharon Belyne Otieno.
The investigation established that an "intimate relationship" had existed between Obado and Otieno, which "subsequently led to a pregnancy with the deceased that the governor was unhappy about."
Both Obado and Otieno's legal teams said they would appeal against the sentence.
His former personal assistant, Michael Oyamo, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison, while former county clerk Caspal Ojwang' Obiero received an 18-year sentence.
The court found that Obado had provided the motive and financial resources for the murder, while Oyamo coordinated its execution and Obiero provided logistical support and helped conceal the crime.
Judge Cecilia Githua said Obado's absence from Migori at the time of the killing did not absolve him of responsibility.
She rejected the prosecution's request for the death penalty, as well as Obado's plea for a non-custodial sentence.
Otieno, 26, was killed between 3 and 4 September 2018 after leaving a hotel in Rongo, south-western Kenya, with journalist Barrack Oduor.
She had contacted Oduor to discuss her relationship with the then-governor. The two were abducted shortly afterwards.
Oduor managed to escape by jumping out of a moving vehicle. His account of the abduction became a crucial lead in the investigation.
Otieno's body was later found near Kodera Forest.
A post-mortem examination found that she had died from strangulation and excessive bleeding caused by multiple stab wounds.
The court also established that Obado was the biological father of her unborn child.
Obado and his co-accused were convicted of murder on 23 July 2026, following a lengthy trial in which prosecutors called 42 witnesses and presented 81 exhibits.
On Friday, the court declined to award compensation to Otieno's family, saying there was insufficient evidence to establish the financial losses they had claimed.
Family plea rejected
Before sentencing, Otieno's mother had appealed to the judge not to send Obado to prison, saying his imprisonment would amount to "another death in the family".
She urged the court to consider a non-custodial sentence, arguing that Otieno's three children, from different relationships, needed his support.
But the judge said the family's circumstances could not override the court's responsibility to impose an appropriate punishment.
Otieno's family, through their lawyer Antony Opondo told Kenya's Daily Nation that they will file an appeal seeking acquittal of Obado.
Otieno's murder sparked protests and renewed public debate about violence against women in Kenya.
A national survey found that at least 34% of women had experienced physical violence in 2022.
The case has also drawn attention because it is rare for such senior political figures to face public criminal trials in Kenya.
Obado served two terms as governor of Migori County in western Kenya, switching allegiance between a smaller political party and the region's dominant opposition movement.
He later backed President William Ruto and formally joined his ruling party in 2023, becoming a regional organiser.

items.title: Israeli attacks on women and girls meant ‘to destroy life’ in Gaza: Amnesty
items.summary:
Israeli attacks on women and girls meant ‘to destroy life’ in Gaza: Amnesty
Israel seeking ‘to prevent births’ and destroy Palestinians in Gaza by targeting women and girls, rights group says.
Israel has sought “to prevent births” in Gaza by repeatedly targeting women and girls, according to Amnesty
items.text:
Israeli attacks on women and girls meant ‘to destroy life’ in Gaza: Amnesty
Israel seeking ‘to prevent births’ and destroy Palestinians in Gaza by targeting women and girls, rights group says.
Israel has sought “to prevent births” in Gaza by repeatedly targeting women and girls, according to Amnesty International.
The rights group said in a report that Israeli forces have killed about 30 women and girls daily since October 2023, while Israel’s blockade on the Strip has led to an untold number of additional female deaths.
The killings, forced displacement, starvation and disruption of critical healthcare services are part of a deliberate drive to prevent the growth of the Palestinian population, the report said – a strategy recognised as constituting genocide.
“Over the past three years, Israel has demonstrated an unending calculated intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza,” Agnes CallamardAgnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International, said.
“Women and girls in Gaza have endured a relentless assault on every aspect of their lives. They have been killed, injured, displaced, starved and denied access to essential healthcare, while systematically stripped of the conditions necessary to make decisions about pregnancy, childbirth and their reproductive futures,” Callamard added.
The report cites harrowing accounts of female survivors who were forced to endure difficult premature births and faced attacks as Israeli forces targeted hospitals caring for incubated babies. Others said they suffered life-altering injuries in attacks, as well as miscarriages and stillbirths.
Israel’s attacks and restrictions have decimated medical infrastructure, cut off access to maternal healthcare, and hampered the flow of medicines and other essential medical needs, the rights group noted.
All nine fertilisation clinics in the enclave have been destroyed, along with eggs and embryos, the report said. Repeated forced displacement orders have further exposed women to gender-based violence.
Preventing births and the intent to destroy life within a group constitute genocide, according to the United Nations’ Genocide Convention.
Amnesty International declared that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza in 2024. Targeting women, girls and reproductive health services was an “integral” part of Israel’s campaign, the group said in its latest report.
Callamard called on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to examine gender-based crimes as part of its ongoing investigation into Israel’s alleged war crimes.
Israel has killed close to 75,000 people in Gaza, according to data from Gaza’s Health Ministry. At least 22,331 women and girls were killed between October 7, 2023 and October 1, 2026, the report said.

items.title: Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
items.summary:
Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
- Published
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.
The troops will hand over security in Luber
items.text:
Uganda to withdraw troops from DR Congo town amid diplomatic row
- Published
Uganda has announced plans to withdraw its troops from a town in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo within two weeks, as diplomatic tensions escalate between the two neighbours.
The troops will hand over security in Lubero, in North Kivu province, to Congolese forces after nearly two years of military operations, the Ugandan army said in a statement on Friday.
The announcement comes days after DR Congo summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over controversial social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is the son of President Yoweri Museveni.
The Ugandan military did not give a reason for the withdrawal or say whether it was linked to the diplomatic row.
The Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) were deployed to Lubero to pursue fighters from the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) Islamist group fleeing joint military operations elsewhere in eastern DR Congo.
The ADF, which originated in Uganda in the 1990s, is affiliated to the Islamic State and has been blamed for numerous deadly attacks on civilians in both countries.
Uganda first deployed troops to eastern DR Congo under the current joint military campaign in November 2021, following a series of bomb attacks in the Ugandan capital, Kampala.
Ugandan army spokesperson Col Chris Magezi said that the joint military campaign, known as Operation Shujaa, would continue elsewhere in DR Congo.
The planned withdrawal applies only to Lubero town.
Five years into the joint offensive, the ADF remains DR Congo's deadliest armed group, despite a significant decline in its activities in Uganda, according to the conflict monitoring organisation Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (Acled).
John Ngono, Acled's DR Congo analyst, said the group was killing an average of four civilians a day and had expanded into previously unaffected parts of eastern DR Congo.
He said the findings suggested that "Operation Shujaa may have improved security in Uganda while shifting the geographical impact of violence within the DRC".
Acled says the group has not carried out an attack in Uganda since June 2025, but its growing interest in mineral resources in DR Congo could help finance its operations and sustain its ability to threaten both countries.
The planned withdrawal comes amid strained relations between Uganda and DR Congo, despite years of close military co-operation.
Earlier this week, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to endorse a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo, threatening that Ugandan troops would seize it themselves if the rebels failed to do so.
The Congolese foreign ministry described his remarks as "particularly serious" and demanded that Uganda clarify its official position and take steps to prevent similar incidents.
Gen Kainerugaba also defended Uganda's military presence in eastern DR Congo, insisting it was driven by security concerns.
The planned withdrawal comes amid renewed fighting between Congolese forces and rebels in the wider Lubero territory, raising fresh concerns about the safety of civilians.
Eastern DR Congo has endured decades of conflict involving dozens of armed groups, with millions of people forced to flee their homes.

items.title: Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
items.summary:
Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
- Published
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkis
items.text:
Clashes mar European games as Macron condemns violence
- Published
Violent clashes marred a number of European football matches on Thursday night, with French president Emmanuel Macron condemning trouble at Marseille's home game against Levski Sofia.
There were also incidents at games between Turkish side Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Be'er-Sheva in Georgia and Sunderland's 1-1 home draw with Poland's Jagiellonia Bialystok.
In Marseille, the build-up to the Europa League match at the Stade Velodrome was affected by incidents in the stands, including the throwing of projectiles and flares between the two sets of supporters.
With 10 minutes to go until kick-off, several Marseille fans ran from a home stand, appearing to pursue a group of Levski Sofia supporters.
They breached the stand designated for away fans, which housed around 500 supporters of the Bulgarian domestic champions.
"Five people were taken to hospital with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder," said the Marseille police prefecture. "Six others were treated on site for various wounds."
Macron spoke to Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev about the incidents, with the French president condemning "with the utmost force these acts of violence, which have no place in sport or in public space", and reassured him that "these acts would not go unpunished".
According to news agency Reuters, Radev thanked Macron for his personal involvement following the "attack on Bulgarian citizens" and for the medical assistance provided to the victims.
Bulgarian President Iliana Iotova said she found video footage of the incidents "shocking" in a statement posted on social media.
"The attacks against the Bulgarian fans desecrate one of the great games that brings millions of people together around the world," she added.
"Everyone should be able to support their team without being afraid for their safety."
Ligue 1 club Marseille said it was "working to understand the precise circumstances of these incidents".
The police source said all the people injured were Bulgarian and there was "no information at this stage regarding any arrests".
Security personnel managed to restore calm, allowing the game to kick-off on time, although there were a few further flare-ups between the fans, notably during the half-time break in a match Marseille won 1-0.
"It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football," said Levski Sofia coach Julio Velazquez
Marseille boss Bruno Genesio added: "We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable."
Meanwhile, the Turkish Football Federation has strongly condemned the "unacceptable" actions of Georgian police towards Besiktas fans who unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during their Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Be'er-Sheva.
Besiktas say they have lodged a complaint with European football's governing body Uefa over "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
The match had been moved from Istanbul to Batumi, Georgia for safety and security reasons but had to be suspended in the 25th minute after clashes involving Besiktas supporters and local police.
Both the officiating team and the Besiktas players left the field, but play was able to resume 30 minutes later.
Besiktas won the match 2-1.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the Uefa Europa League match," said a statement from the Turkish federation.
Turkish outlet NTV reported that Georgian police had gone into the stands and used pepper spray on the Besiktas fans.
The report added that there were anti-Israeli chants from the Turkish fans and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters to try to calm matters before play restarted.
Hakan Fidan, Turkey's minister of foreign affairs, spoke to his Georgian counterpart Maka Botchorishvili following the incident.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
At Sunderland, there were crowd disturbances after Jagiellonia Bialystok fans were found in areas of the Stadium of Light with home fans, despite Uefa having imposed an away supporter ban for the Europa League game.
Police and stewards attended some disruption early on during the match.
"In the build-up to the match, the club had put measures in place in line with this sanction and maintained regular communication with our supporters, Jagiellonia Bialystok and Uefa," said a Sunderland statement.
"Unfortunately, Jagiellonia Bialystok failed to engage and cooperate on this matter.
"We are disappointed that these measures and communications were disregarded by some visiting supporters and we will review the circumstances surrounding their entry into the stadium."
