items.title: 'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry
items.summary:
'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry
- Published
"I don't want to shut out the noise, we just need to know that it's coming and it's going to be electric."
The "noise" Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert refers to has been building over recent weeks, with 'Spygate' returning
items.text:
'Massive for both' - Saints and Boro revisit Spygate rivalry
- Published
"I don't want to shut out the noise, we just need to know that it's coming and it's going to be electric."
The "noise" Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert refers to has been building over recent weeks, with 'Spygate' returning to the collective consciousness as Saints and Middlesbrough meet on Friday (20:00 GMT) for the first time since the scandal.
The most recent time they came face-to-face was in last season's Championship play-off semi-finals.
Saints ended up winning over the two legs, but were then expelled from the final having being caught spying on a Boro training session before the first match at the Riverside.
It turned into a five-month saga which started with a Saints performance analyst being photographed from behind a tree, and ended with Eckert being handed a suspended ban and fined £28,000.
The German head coach signed a new deal at Saints exactly a week ago and previously admitted the experience of Spygate had changed his life.
Now St Mary's awaits as the two sides will re-ignite their rivalry after a tough end to the last campaign for both.
Saints players felt aggrieved for not being allowed to feature in the play-off final, while Boro suffered the heartbreak of losing at Wembley, as Hull City won promotion to the Premier League.
"It's a massive game for both teams," former Nottingham Forest and Ipswich defender Luke Chambers told the 72+ podcast.
"Middlesbrough have bounced back tremendously well from the play-offs, the ups and downs, they didn't know if they were coming or going, and to go through that heartache of making the final and not getting over the line - credit to them.
"It will be an electric atmosphere and there will be added needle on the pitch, especially with some of the things that happened in the games between the two sides last season when the news broke out."
- Hellberg reveals Eckert apology after Spygate 
  - Published8 October
- Southampton give head coach Eckert new deal 
  - Published6 days ago
- 'It's changed my life' - Eckert on Spygate scandal 
  - Published8 October
Hellberg and Eckert ready to move on - but can supporters?
Boro boss Kim Hellberg and Eckert both arrived at their respective clubs in November 2025 and have enjoyed plenty of success on the pitch over the past 12 months.
But following the 2-1 defeat in May's play-off semi-final second leg at St Mary's, Hellberg described it as "one of the toughest days" in his coaching career.
Although Friday's game promises to be filled with emotion on the pitch and in the stands, the two head coaches claim to have made up since the events of last season after Eckert called Hellberg to apologise over the summer.
"We spoke and he called me. I've always been a person who wants to give people a second chance," Hellberg told BBC Radio Tees.
"He has also gone though some things that have been very tough for him in terms of this which is something you don't wish anyone.
"I think in general for me it's overplayed. We have talked about it, everything has been sorted and now I'm looking forward to playing against a good side with a good manager and see how good we can be, and I'm really looking forward to it."
After Eckert took responsibility and apologised over the summer, both he and the club also expressed a desire to move on after the backing of the Saints board and owner Dragan Solak.
Some members of the Middlesbrough press have been robust and consistent in their strong criticism of Southampton and Eckert since Spygate first emerged.
Eckert had walked out of media conferences during the play-off semi-final following some stern questioning of him, while a piece was published on Thursday which questioned the German's character.
On Friday, Southampton published their own video, external on club channels, emotionally recalling the play-off campaign and how success was "ours... until it wasn't" before Boro "got another go", followed by footage of Oli McBurnie's winner for Hull at Wembley.
"People talk about last season, but we're focused on this one," narrates Southampton-based streamer Tyrone, over clips of goals from this season. "And now, here we are again; new hope, more reasons to believe, the same leader. We know all eyes are on us, and we're ready."
Southampton fan Rob Maddox echoed the emotions of both managers and felt that the majority of both fanbases want to now put the previous distaste behind them.
"There has been so much football since the play-off semi-final that I think both clubs are ready to get on with it now," he said.
"Some might look to hype the game up as a rivalry but I think the game should be looked at as two very good footballing sides going head to head.
"Of course there is going to be that little bit of spice and I'm sure we'll see it in the stands, but I hope that after the game we're talking about both teams showing off what they can do on the pitch."
Boro fan Jack McBride agreed that "Spygate's over and done with now" but admitted there was still a feeling of "bitterness" within the fanbases.
"I've seen some back and forth which is fun and all part of being a football fan, but there's also the other side of it which is bitter, twisted and they're still going on about it in a negative way," he told BBC Radio Tees.
"We had our chance and we didn't take it. Saints have had a four-point deduction, Tonda's been punished, we move on. Was it enough? Personally, I don't think that it was but we move on from it.
"This is a game we've all been looking to, and it was probably the first fixture that Boro and Saints fans were looking for.
"I think it's going to be quite a hostile atmosphere. I think Saints will be booing constantly and Boro fans will bring the noise as much as they can."

items.title: Can Borussia Dortmund finally end their title wait? Three big questions for Bundesliga leaders
items.summary: Borussia Dortmund’s dreams have a habit of becoming nightmares, like when they somehow handed Bayern Munich the Bundesliga title on the final day of the 2022-23 season. Or when an 89th-minute Arjen Robben goal won the 2013 Champions League final for the same opponents. Whenever Dortmund suffer heart
items.text:
Borussia Dortmund’s dreams have a habit of becoming nightmares, like when they somehow handed Bayern Munich the Bundesliga title on the final day of the 2022-23 season. Or when an 89th-minute Arjen Robben goal won the 2013 Champions League final for the same opponents. Whenever Dortmund suffer heartbreak, it usually involves Bayern.
As things stand, however, Niko Kovac’s side hold a two-point lead over Bayern at the top of the Bundesliga. Both teams are unbeaten, but Dortmund may be the more stable of the two at the moment, especially with Harry Kane expected to miss several months through injury.
So can Dortmund make the most of this opportunity to become German champions for the first time since the Jürgen Klopp era? Or is another Dortmund dream destined to end in disappointment?
Will the data catch up with Dortmund?
The table never lies, apparently. The underlying data, however, can call into question the sustainability of a team’s position and, right now, it is casting serious doubt on Dortmund’s Bundesliga title prospects.
Dortmund rank a lowly 13th for expected goals (xG). Seven Bundesliga teams have scored more goals than the leaders, whose lack of open-play creativity is in stark contrast to that of Bayern’s – the Bavarians have scored 30 goals in 10 games and are still underperforming their own xG.
These attacking numbers haven’t been an issue for Dortmund given their defensive strength. Indeed, they are the most resolute defensive unit in the league, keeping more clean sheets than any other side. Having conceded only seven goals from an xG against of 13.4, though, there could be a correction coming.
The difference between Dortmund’s attacking and defensive stats is stark. While Ramy Bensebaini ranks in the top 10 for defensive contributions per 90 minutes this season, Dortmund do not have a single player in the top 30 for chances created. Fábio Silva is their most prolific shot-taker and he’s ranked 27th for shots per 90 minutes. This lack of statistical balance could be an issue over a full season.
Have Bayern’s injuries opened the door?
For Dortmund to win their first Bundesliga title in 15 years, they need Bayern to have an off season. That may be materialising such is the number of injuries the Bundesliga champions are having to handle right now.
Luis Díaz, Serge Gnabry and Manuel Neuer have all missed a large portion of the season while Ismael Saibari, Michael Olise and Alphonso Davies have also been absent through injury as Jamal Musiala continues to recover from a neurological condition. Most significant, though, is Kane’s absence. The Ballon d’Or winner, sidelined for a lengthy spell after undergoing surgery on torn ankle ligaments sustained in Bayern’s 1-1 draw with Cologne on Friday, has scored an incredible 156 goals in 163 appearances over the last four seasons and is Bayern’s creative heart. Without him, Vincent Kompany’s team simply do not pose the same threat, which was evident in this week’s Champions League loss to Lille.
Dortmund have injury troubles of their own. Giannis Konstantelias is out for the rest of the season after undergoing ACL surgery in September while Emre Can has not played since the spring. Compared to Bayern Munich’s crock list, though, there is not much for Kovac to worry about.
What can Dortmund learn from Leverkusen?
Bayer Leverkusen were the last team to disrupt Bayern Munich’s domestic dominance, winning the 2023-24 Bundesliga title under Xabi Alonso. Just like Dortmund, Leverkusen had a reputation for being perennial bridesmaids – indeed they were nicknamed “Neverkusen” for decades. That season, though, Alonso’s team demolished the rest of the competition, finishing a massive 17 points ahead of the chasing pack on the back of not losing a single game.
Leverkusen did not become nervous down the stretch because they were so far ahead from so early on. There is a lesson in that for Dortmund. They simply must capitalize on any Bayern Munich weakness while they can.
Under Alonso, Leverkusen were relentless. They played with intensity in every match and had an approach that reflected the ideals of their then up-and-coming manager. The BayArena was an exciting place to be and that came across in the energy of the team on the pitch. Dortmund have a different sort of energy, but Kovac has instilled a strong set of principles in his players and Dortmund’s form this season is a clear continuation of Kovac’s project. The Westfalenstadion faithful has ever reason to be hopeful once again.

items.title: Brighton's perfect blend: The duo key to Seagulls' rise
items.summary:
Pascal Gross and Luka Vuskovic helping drive Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton and their stunning Premier League start
There's a 16-year age gap between Gross, 35, and Vuskovic, 19, but the pair have been central to the stunning start Brighton have made to the Premier League; watch Brighton vs Newcastle li
items.text:
Pascal Gross and Luka Vuskovic helping drive Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton and their stunning Premier League start
There's a 16-year age gap between Gross, 35, and Vuskovic, 19, but the pair have been central to the stunning start Brighton have made to the Premier League; watch Brighton vs Newcastle live on Sky Sports Premier League on Sunday; kick-off 2.05pm
Thursday 26 November 2026 13:05, UK
It was a painful Sunday afternoon at Hull, but by the time Brighton pair Luka Vuskovic and Pascal Gross arrived at the beachside restaurant on Tuesday, you got the impression they didn't need too much of the bracing near-frozen sea air to boost the mood.
Yes, they were disappointed, but they weren't going to let a few minutes and Oli McBurnie overshadow a start to the season that has taken the Seagulls second in the Premier League table after 11 games.
Not many would have predicted such a lofty position for Fabian Hurzeler's team - including some of the Brighton team themselves - but the club are playing some thrilling football, and the 26 goals they have scored has helped them beat the likes of Arsenal and Man City already this season.

Sitting in front of me are two of the reasons why. They are both too modest to entertain that, but at the heart of this side's success is an almost seamless tactical and generational blend epitomised by Gross and Vuskovic.
Gross has been a revelation since his return earlier this year, something he admits he was nervous about doing. "You always hope for the best, but you never know. Coming back is not always easy."
The German international is making it look effortless. Opta have the 35-year-old top of their running stats, with 131.5km covered so far this league season, and only Declan Rice has more assists (4 vs 5).
But Gross' influence can't only be measured in numbers; this anchor or "connector" - as Hurzeler likes to call him - goes far beyond. No wonder his contract was recently extended for another season.
"I love the place, a lot of important things in my life happened here," he says.
"I have my family here, my kids are happy, my dog... it's a beautiful place with a lot of special people, where I feel really connected, really comfortable with the whole culture.
"We have so much talent and we have a lot of good people, but from different backgrounds. So that's really challenging, but I love the challenge because they're all good people we have in the dressing room.
"I was, at one point, a guy who came from another country, but I wanted to adapt, I wanted to be part of the culture. You need to help and support the guys. I really believe in what the club is doing. I think I can be a big part on and off the pitch."
The German international returned to Brighton after his dream move to Borussia Dortmund - the club he supported as a boy - ended early. He was desperate to show he could still perform at the highest level consistently. "I had to prove a point for myself, but also I wanted to repay the trust the club showed in me."
Do you remember playing better at any point in your career, I ask, telling him The Athletic had him as their number one player of the season so far.
"I don't believe in that. I don't see it like that. Maybe our start and the little things getting over-exaggerated.
"I think I am playing at my best, but maybe I think I'm a very good player in a good group who's working well, because everybody is improving. The way we set up, the way we play, I think everybody looks good."
Those stats, I say, are remarkable and again he down plays the praise. But he does concede: "They are really good, but because the team is playing well. If the team is playing well, everybody individually maybe looks a bit better."
Gross is honest enough to admit the start has surprised him. "No, I wouldn't say I expected that. I always hope for the best, but I know every game, like we saw on the weekend, is so different and so difficult that momentum can change quick."
Now, he says, comes the big challenge: the busy period. "It's a different sport, I always say". But you get the sense Brighton will be ready for it.
Alongside Gross, Vukovic has been another of the central characters in Brighton's success this season. He arrived in the summer from Tottenham in a club record deal worth £46m.
Vuskovic is no stranger to breaking records - two days after his 16th birthday, he became the youngest player to feature in Croatia's top flight. He is the fourth generation of his family to play football. Defending is very much the family business.
At 19, he has already played football in Croatia, Germany, Belgium and Poland, which has certainly helped him prepare for life as a central defender in the Premier League.
He says: "When you join as a 30-year-old guy, compared to say 15, instantly you have to grow up, you have to realise something in your life, and you have to mature.
"I had a really good group of people at Hajduk Split that made me mature fast enough, and they really helped me. In each of the countries, it was very helpful to develop, to grow as a human, as a football player."
Vuskovic's form in these first few months of the season has prompted a few questions about why Spurs let him leave in the summer and brought in Brighton's Paul van Hecke.
He doesn't see it as "rejection" and appreciates everything they did for him but, he adds: "In the end the coach came and said he didn't see me in his system, which is completely normal in football. I think in the end everybody earned (something). I gained experience, I moved to another club and I think we are all very happy about it.

items.title: The English Lamine Yamal? Why Williams-Barnett is getting Spurs fans excited
items.summary:
Why Tottenham's Luca Williams-Barnett earned Lamine Yamal comparisons from Roberto De Zerbi
Sky Sports' Callum Bishop takes a look into Tottenham's next big hope Luca Williams-Barnett after the teenager signed a new long-term deal at the club; watch Sunderland vs Tottenham live on Sky Sports Main Ev
items.text:
Why Tottenham's Luca Williams-Barnett earned Lamine Yamal comparisons from Roberto De Zerbi
Sky Sports' Callum Bishop takes a look into Tottenham's next big hope Luca Williams-Barnett after the teenager signed a new long-term deal at the club; watch Sunderland vs Tottenham live on Sky Sports Main Event on Super Sunday; kick-off 2.05pm
Wednesday 25 November 2026 14:13, UK
To earn comparisons to Lamine Yamal after just three Premier League appearances might seem a little far-fetched, but Roberto De Zerbi showed no hesitation.
So highly thought of is Luca Williams-Barnett at Tottenham that the remarks made following his stellar performance in the 2-0 win over Ipswich weren't all that shocking to hear.
"Luca is a special player. I'm not surprised because his talent is bigger than you think," De Zerbi said before simply saying, "yes, I think so," when asked if he could reach Lamine Yamal's level.

- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract
The 18-year-old wouldn't even be halfway through his second year of A-levels, but his talent hasn't been a secret. The likes of Bayern Munich and Manchester United had already been linked with the starlet, so the news of a long-term contract at Spurs is one that brings unbridled joy among the fanbase.
An England U19 international, Williams-Barnett made plenty of headlines in his first start. Most notably, he became Tottenham's third-youngest Premier League goalscorer at 18 years and 51 days, only four days older than Gareth Bale, who is second on the list. That name certainly rings a bell.
The winger was also Spurs' sixth-youngest Premier League starter, and it's not just with his club that he's making history.
Just three other players have scored on their first Premier League start at a younger age, while he is only bettered by future Ballon d'Or winner Michael Owen as the youngest player to score and grab an assist in the same game.
The records are a great indicator of the talent that the youngster has. Famous Spurs wonderkids such as Harry Kane, Dele Alli and Glenn Hoddle had yet to make an impact at that age.
But what is it about his game that is really making people stand up and take notice?
De Zerbi said after the Ipswich victory that he asked Williams-Barnett "to play like he plays at the park with his friends, with the same freedom".
It's the sort of cliché that you often hear levelled at emerging talents. Where they often lack in experience and nuance, they make up for in fearlessness and often youthful abandon.
De Zerbi's request was never going to be a challenge for the teenager, though. That trait is what had already earned him admirers from those in the know.
"He deserves the opportunity to play. He's got the swagger, he's got the ability to play in that team," was Tim Sherwood's assessment before he had even kicked a ball this season.
While the swagger can't be denied, his trademark on the pitch is rather straightforward. Williams-Barnett's tendency is to slow the play down and keep the ball close to his feet before showing explosive acceleration to catch his marker off guard.
Though it isn't necessarily the most groundbreaking piece of skill, the youngster possesses an abundance of composure that sees him capable of going on the inside or outside. Something that Anan Khalaili found out the hard way during the youngster's cameo against Crystal Palace.
It's the sort of foundational skill that gave the likes of Ronaldinho and Neymar a platform to develop into the greatest flair players of their generation. Funny that Williams-Barnett should bear some resemblance considering the Brazilian duo appear to play a role in his pre-match routine.
"I've seen today in the bus from the training ground to the stadium, because he was very close with me, while we were coming in the stadium, he was watching on YouTube Ronaldinho, [Eden] Hazard, Neymar," De Zerbi disclosed after the Ipswich win.
He is clearly taking inspiration from what he has seen from these idols. If we are being critical of those superstars, the one thing the youngster might want to avoid adopting from them is their desire off the ball, as his head coach has already challenged him to.
"Work hard without the ball, like [Ousmane] Dembele, like Raphinha, like [Lamine] Yamal, because football is going in a different way and the first defenders are the attackers. Even if they are Ballon d'Or winners, or any players with talent, they have to work on the pitch."
To that degree, the gauntlet has been set by De Zerbi. But there is no doubting that Williams-Barnett has the backing of those at Spurs to go and make himself a huge success.
"What stands out most for me is his courage and bravery because as a young lad coming into Spurs first team and performing like that is not easy. He will have a very big future," said team-mate Omar Marmoush.
It has been over a decade since the club had a youth product that has captured the imagination in quite this way. Kane is the most obvious example, but not even he immediately made fans pay attention to this extent.
As is the case with every young player, patience is a virtue. But with a new contract, De Zerbi's blessing and a start to Premier League life that could hardly go any better, the sky is the limit for Williams-Barnett.
It is far too early to say exactly how far he goes. But if he shoots for the moon and misses, he will still become one of the stars.

items.title: Tarik Muharemovic: ‘Dad is at every Leeds game. I sometimes hear him shouting from the stands’
items.summary:
Tarik Muharemovic is proving one of the best signings of this Premier League season and there will be special resonance when his upwardly mobile Leeds side host Coventry on Saturday.
Whereas Muharemovic’s father, Rasim, has been a matchday regular since the defender’s £34.1m move from Sassuolo, his
items.text:
Tarik Muharemovic is proving one of the best signings of this Premier League season and there will be special resonance when his upwardly mobile Leeds side host Coventry on Saturday.
Whereas Muharemovic’s father, Rasim, has been a matchday regular since the defender’s £34.1m move from Sassuolo, his mother, Elmedina, will watch her son play for Leeds for the first time.
The 6ft 4in Bosnia and Herzegovina centre-half credits his parents for a rise which has taken him to Wolfsberger in Austria and Juventus and Sassuolo in Italy before he joined Daniel Farke’s side in July. Rasim and Elmedina fled war in their homeland and moved to Slovenia, where Muharemovic and his brother, Kenan, were born.
“My whole story is down to my parents and everything I do is for them,” says the articulate 23-year-old, who speaks five languages and represented Bosnia at this year’s World Cup. “I think about them leaving their home, their family and friends and it was because of a war.
“Bosnia was in a bad situation; the whole of Yugoslavia was in a bad situation so they had to leave. They went to live in Slovenia for three years before moving to Austria because there were better jobs and more opportunities.
“My parents live there now but it’s still not easy when they look back at leaving their home and friends … yet they had to. They do everything for me and Kenan, who is at Rapid Vienna in Austria. He’s only 20 and some of my friends and family say he could be a bigger talent than me. He’s also a left-footed centre-back and we speak every day.”
During Muharemovic’s childhood, his father was relentless in helping him to realise his potential and not much has changed. “My dad would always be there asking: ‘Tarik, if you want to be the best, why didn’t you do this?’” Muharemovic says. “He pushed me to the limits, he was always there on the sidelines and still is now at every Leeds game. I can sometimes hear him shouting from the stands.”
Muharemovic quickly rose to prominence at Wolfsberger and after six first-team appearances he signed for Juventus aged 18 in 2021. He trained with the revered defenders Giorgio Chiellini and Leonardo Bonucci but a first-team appearance eluded Muharemovic and he joined Sassuolo, then in Serie B, initially on loan, in August 2024.
That proved the making of him as they were promoted as champions and Muharemovic thrived under Fabio Grosso’s guidance. He says: “Juventus was the best defensive school with a coach in Massimo Allegri who focused a lot on training and tactics and players like Chiellini and Bonucci.
“As a teenager, it was a privilege to train with these guys because they tell you everything you need to do. Chiellini would celebrate slide tackles and winning duels during games, so I like to do that too because my emotion comes out.
“I’ve always closely followed Virgil van Dijk’s defending and Edin Dzeko is a big idol of mine as a legend of Bosnian football. I’m very honoured and proud to have had such special moments with him, especially representing Bosnia together at the World Cup.”
Muharemovic’s World Cup experiences included a red card against Switzerland and being the victim of a challenge by Folarin Balogun which led to the USA forward being sent off, only for his one-game ban to be suspended by Fifa after an intervention by Donald Trump. The summer also brought interest from Inter and speculation about a return to Juventus before Leeds signed him on a five-year deal.
“I had a few teams interested in me but the dream has always been to play in the Premier League,” says Muharemovic, who captained Bosnia for the first time against Romania this month. “I had an amazing call with the boss [Farke] about the project at Leeds and just had to say yes. He’s built a family here and there’s a huge togetherness with all the players, staff and fans.”
Leeds thumped Chelsea 4-1 last weekend in their first win at Stamford Bridge since 1999, prompting talk of a push for European qualification. They have not conceded in the opening 22 minutes in the past 43 matches and belief is growing.
“We all dream about Europe and playing on the big stage,” says Muharemovic, whose performances for Leeds have attracted admiring glances across the continent. “It would be very deserved and special if we can do it for us as players, the fans and the club … I’m just happy with what I’m doing for me and my family and to show those people who didn’t believe in me that I can do it.
“Everyone knows the Premier League is the most difficult league in football but I never doubted myself. I know my qualities and I’m having a good season but it’s very early so I just need to keep playing consistently.”
Looking ahead to his parents’ visit, Muharemovic, a Muslim who prays five times a day, says: “It’ll be very emotional when I see them together at Elland Road for the first time. My dad has been to every game so far and was in the away end in the opening match at Nottingham Forest. I thought the families would sit in a different part of the ground, so when I saw him sat with the Leeds supporters as I was warming up, I was like: ‘Oh my God, good luck!’
“I know what Leeds fans are like so I was thinking: ‘I just hope no one jumps over him,’ but he absolutely loves it. Now my mum is coming too, it’s special and I can’t wait so hopefully we can celebrate with another win. Yes, I’m living the dream but I’m just getting started and always want to show more and achieve more.”

items.title: Everyone keeps linking USMNT players to Man United: Could an American help the club?
items.summary:

items.text:
If you follow the U.S. men's national team, here's a good sanity check: Imagine going back in time -- say, 15 years -- and telling your past self about the current situation.
"Yeah, so there's this guy who came up through the FC Dallas academy, moved to Schalke when he was a kid, started for them as an 18-year-old when they finished second in the Bundesliga behind Bayern Munich, and then moved to Juventus. He has played more Serie A matches for Juve than anyone else in the seven seasons since he joined the team."
"And he just did this news conference where he said, 'Guys from here being talked about going to Manchester United' was 'inevitable.' Oh, and this is important: he was saying that because Manchester United just poached the USMNT manager in the middle of the Premier League season."
Think about all the assumptions your 15-years-younger self would be making, whenever they had regained consciousness after suffering the double-whammy of learning that time travel exists and that the USMNT was one step below Manchester United in the global pecking order.
... Schalke are one of the best development clubs in the world, and Juventus are one of the best clubs in the world, so one of the best soccer players in the world plays for the USMNT now? And then, well, the USMNT coach is now coaching Manchester United, which might be the best club in the world. If my math is right, then there was a World Cup a couple of months ago -- in summer 2026 -- so ... wait ... did the U.S. just win the World Cup?
At this point, you'd disappear back to the present, allowing yourself to dream of a more hopeful future -- rather than explaining what happened to the Italian economy in the aughts, or what went down at Manchester United after Sir Alex Ferguson left, or what the USMNT's score against Belgium was.
But even with the relative changes in station over the past decade-plus, it's still a surreal thing to say today: Manchester United just hired away the USMNT manager. And, as Weston McKennie suggested, this always happens: Transfer rumors connect the manager of a new club with a smattering of players from the manager's old team.
All of which brings us here: Would any of Mauricio Pochettino's former players actually make Manchester United better? And even if they would, should United sign any of them?
What do Manchester United need?
There are three clear, interrelated issues with the way United's team plays and the way United's team was built.
The first: They're old. In fact, they're as old as Arsenal.
Now, you might be saying, "But Arsenal are the best team in the league!" But, well, Arsenal are the best team in the league, in part, because they're old. After multiple seasons of signing exclusively young players, they've spent the past two years adding established players who are late in their prime to the roster. They are trying to win as much as possible right now, and so their average age, weighted by minutes played, is 27.2 -- tied for third oldest in the league.
Although they finished third last season, United were clearly not a title contender coming into the Premier League season -- and, well, they're currently in 19th place. After Sunday's embarrassing loss to Liverpool, prediction markets now give them a 19% chance of being relegated. Once again, this team should be building for future title contention -- not contention to win right now.
Perhaps connected to that is the team's inability or unwillingness to press. The stats app Futi measures team's tendencies across a variety of stylistic markers. One of which is: "Stay compact to deny space or press to win the ball during the opponent's buildup?" Here's where United landed on that spectrum before Pochettino took over:
It's even worse when you look at what they do soon after possession is turned over: "Press aggressively to win back lost balls or fall back to recover defensive structure?"
While the league has moved toward a much more aggressive stance in these situations, United have gone in the opposite direction:
And it hasn't helped the defense in any way.
Only one team has conceded more expected goals than United this season:
We know that Pochettino wants his teams to press, and we know that pressing tends to favor younger, more energetic, and more mobile players. We also know that Pochettino's USMNT ticked both of these boxes at the World Cup: They were one of the more aggressive pressing teams in the tournament, and -- despite the presence of 39-year-old Tim Ream -- the ninth-youngest team in the field, weighted by minutes played.
Would any USMNT players make Man United better?
Given everything we've just gone over -- or, you know, what you might've watched Sunday -- the obvious place to start is in the back.
Man United goalkeeper Senne Lammens is young and roughly a league-average Premier League starter, and goalkeeper might be the weakest position in the USMNT pool. No Americans would be an upgrade here.
At the back, United's four most-used players this season are Diogo Dalot at right back, Luke Shaw at left back, and Harry Maguire and Lisandro Martínez at center back. Shaw is 31, Maguire 33, Martinez 28 -- and they're all out of contract at the end of this season. Plus, a large chunk of the defensive issues can probably be directed here.
These players are all on the older side, and none of them are above-average or even average ground-covering athletes. It's really hard for a team to press without rangy defenders covering behind the press, but none of these defenders have excelled in the more passive defensive structure. Otherwise, well, United wouldn't give up so many great chances.
Pochettino seemed aware of this, as he benched Maguire for the Liverpool match and played a back three with the theoretically more mobile Leny Yoro and Matthijs De Ligt alongside Martinez. We just needed eight minutes of game time at Anfield to see that this probably isn't the solution.

items.title: 'Man Utd being relegated would be the biggest shock in history... but it won't happen'
items.summary:
Man Utd being relegated would be the biggest shock in history, but it won't happen, says Paul Merson
Manchester United take on Brentford on Saturday with Mauricio Pochettino looking for his first win to take them out of the relegation zone; Arsenal then take on Man City, live on Sky Sports this Sund
items.text:
Man Utd being relegated would be the biggest shock in history, but it won't happen, says Paul Merson
Manchester United take on Brentford on Saturday with Mauricio Pochettino looking for his first win to take them out of the relegation zone; Arsenal then take on Man City, live on Sky Sports this Sunday, the reigning champions are aiming to go nine points clear of Enzo Maresca's side
Friday 27 November 2026 09:20, UK
In his latest Sky Sports column, Paul Merson previews a big weekend for Manchester United, before Arsenal take on Manchester City in a huge game live this Sunday.
Mauricio Pochettino is looking for his first win as United boss as he bids to take them out of the relegation zone. However, Brentford visit Old Trafford on the back of their recent win over Everton, which took them into the top six.
- Premier League Predictor - play our new game
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
Then on Sunday, Arsenal host title rivals Man City. Enzo Maresca's side are already six points behind the reigning champions and have won just two out of their last seven matches in all competitions.
Read below for the Magic Man's thoughts ahead of a huge weekend in the Premier League...
'Brentford game is massive for Man Utd'
Manchester United are in trouble. 100 per cent. Of course they are. But I don't see them getting relegated, absolutely not.
I would be shocked and amazed, it would be the biggest shock in the history of anything. People will go: Mike Tyson got beat by Buster Douglas. But that was one punch. This is over 38 games.
Brentford is a massive football match for them. If they lost that game, I don't see them beating Newcastle if Matthias Jaissle's side get anywhere near the level they played against Arsenal in the second half.
Then by the time you're playing Coventry, you're more than a win away from getting out of trouble. As soon as that starts happening, that's when it starts getting worrying - when you need two weeks to get out of the bottom three, or four or five points away.
The next three weeks are massive for United. If they beat Brentford this week, that will settle them down.
But I look at the teams down there right now. Crystal Palace won't go to Old Trafford and win. Sunderland and Nottingham Forest won't. Fulham and Coventry won't. Hull won't. So that means to me that Man Utd are better than them.
That's why I don't see them getting relegated. When you look at it like that, there are a lot of worse teams than them.
Man Utd have bought too many 'four or nines' - that's what I call them. They're either 4/10 or 9/10. They're not in between. You can't do that at Man Utd. You have to be between a seven or an eight on a consistent basis. You can't be four one week and nine the next, it doesn't work.
The pace of the game is controlled by the other team, it's never controlled by Manchester United.
They have got no defenders. They've gone it horribly wrong, trying to build from front to back. But it's more than that, it's spine of the team.
They need a centre forward. They don't have a dictating midfield player who comes short and controls the game. The only way United can do that is if they sacrifice Fernandes going forward and playing him deeper, like a quarterback - and then hope you've got enough going forwards elsewhere.
I don't see anyone else in that United team who is capable of coming deep and playing the ball forward. Playing that pass on a consistent basis, making the right decisions.
'Man City have lost their fear factor'
Man City have got to go out and play for the fans, they're the ones who are paying their money. They're getting paid £300,000-a-week, the fans are the ones paying to watch them.
Man City are getting a little bit found out. I have always said, even when they were playing at their best, they give you chances. And you have to make those chances count.
It used to be: go to the Etihad, get your stomach's tickled, get out with a 3-0 defeat that you're more than happy with that, and go back on the coach - because they could win games by six or seven.
Then all of a sudden, they started winning games but they were also open at the same time. And now, teams don't fear them.
Teams know they will get chances if they have a go at them - and enough chances to win football matches, not just one or two chances.
If you are brave enough - like Fulham were by getting players in the opposition box - you can beat Man City.
This is the problem for them: they're too open and there's not that fear factor anymore. And I also don't think Erling Haaland gets the service he deserves.
You would like to think that City's players aren't being affected by the charges hanging over them, because no one knows what is going to happen. So you have to play until you know what's going to happen.
It's like life: no one's going to tell you what's going to happen tomorrow, so live today.
'If Arsenal beat Man City, the league could be over soon'
If Arsenal win this game, the league is finished. That would be nine points clear and this league could be over very, very quickly.
Arsenal were dominant in the first half against Newcastle and if it was a boxing match, then Newcastle would have thrown the towel in.
They came out the second half a bit lackadaisical and Newcastle were outstanding by playing on the front foot. But then Arsenal switched and decided they weren't going to lose.
And then they scored one of the best goals of the season. If the finish from Noni Madueke was good, it would be the goal of the season. But when you see the finish, it's not great and the goalkeeper should save it. If he whips it into the far corner, it's goal of the season.
I think we saw enough with Brighton last weekend against Hull. That's one of those games where you go: if you can't win it, don't lose it.
You feel sorry for Brighton, because Konstantinos Tzolakis was unreal. He should be playing for the New York Rangers t

items.text:
Guinea-Bissau's military leaders delay return to civilian rule until 2028
- Published
Guinea-Bissau's military rulers have postponed elections scheduled for next week by two years, delaying the return to civilian rule.
Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the presidential and parliamentary elections, originally due on 6 December, would now take place on 26 November 2028.
The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, promising to return the country to civilian rule within 12 months.
In a statement, the presidency said an assessment of electoral preparations had found that there were insufficient "technical, material and financial conditions" to hold the polls as planned.
It said the delay would provide more time to ensure the elections were credible, transparent and inclusive, with all candidates given equal opportunities.
The presidency also reiterated its commitment to holding the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date for the vote.
Gen N'Tam was sworn in as transitional president a day after the military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embaló in November 2025.
The coup took place three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due to be announced.
Both Embaló and his main challenger, Fernando Dias, had claimed victory.
Embaló, who has since been living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning to Guinea-Bissau last month, despite expressing an interest in contesting the elections.
Guinea-Bissau has experienced several coups and attempted coups since gaining independence from Portugal in 1974.

items.title: Liam Delap’s struggles are symbolic of damaging Chelsea churn
items.summary: Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea ma
items.text:
Liam Delap came and went. He joined Chelsea in the summer of 2025 and was hailed by Enzo Maresca as the next Harry Kane. Fast forward a year, though, and there was no chance of Delap joining Kane in England’s World Cup squad. The striker’s form was miserable and the only surprise was that Chelsea made a profit when they sold him to Nottingham Forest for £50m last summer.
On one level it looks like good business. Delap’s only season at Stamford Bridge featured one serious hamstring injury, one league goal, one ridiculous red card and not much else. Analysts at other clubs rated him at Ipswich and felt Chelsea was the wrong fit for his direct style of play. The mistake was less the decision not to give Delap another season, no matter the worries over cover for João Pedro, more the call to sign him in the first place.
At the same time, however, Delap’s experience speaks to the questions around culture and identity dogging Chelsea before they face Forest and their former striker at the City Ground on Friday night. It is a point that could be applied to so many of the players to join during this ownership’s four years in charge. Alejandro Garnacho, languishing on loan at Aston Villa, was a £40m signing last year, and only three of the 12 players who joined in the 2024-25 season are still at the club.
There is a constant churn. Laurence Stewart has departed the five-strong sporting director team and there also are whispers around Dave Fallows, although insiders insist there will be no further changes. Back to the squad and Moisés Caicedo, Roméo Lavia and Cole Palmer are the only survivors from the 2023-24 intake. Wesley Fofana, Malo Gusto and Gaga Slonina remain from the 16 who joined in the 2022-23 season. The trading is relentless and, although the ability to raise funds meant Chelsea were in position to spend £117m on Morgan Rogers last summer, it is hard not to wonder whether the strategy has hindered the team’s development.
The lack of consistency was evident when Chelsea lost 4-1 at home to Leeds last Saturday. Xabi Alonso, whose side are eighth after five defeats in their first 11 league games, has focused on raising standards. But shifting mindset is harder when the players cannot fall back on a clear identity. The chopping and changing has consequences. Reece James, Chelsea’s captain, is the only first-teamer who represented the club during the Roman Abramovich era. It is not a surprise that supporters feel little connection to the players. Fans wonder whether the long contracts handed out to players have meaning. They hear Fofana appear to joke about missing a penalty against Liverpool and wonder whether the players care. It explains why the atmosphere at Stamford Bridge quickly grows toxic. The culture has to change. There has to be more accountability.
“This is a goal for us – that we are able to have stability, to be more competitive,” Alonso said on Thursday. “For me, to build that core, to build that way of doing things, it’s very important for the newcomers when you really get into the place and you know how things work.”
It is a work in progress. The final whistle against Leeds brought the sight of Palmer, who is horribly out of form, arguing with João Pedro and Willie Isa, the player support and development officer, about refusing to acknowledge the fans. There has been more woe this week, the mood soured by Fofana’s ill-advised chat with a French YouTuber. Fofana has had to apologise after failing to seek club permission for an interview in which he revealed that he almost quit football before his agents pointed out how much money was left on his contract.
Alonso, who refused to say whether the £75m defender had been fined, was unamused. “He apologised,” the manager said. “He knows it was not right. We are here to take things seriously.”
The worry is that Chelsea still look unserious. They have plenty to prove after being bullied by Leeds and Sunderland. Delap, who has been finetuning his heading in training this week, will fancy his chances after Fofana and Levi Colwill toiled against target men when they faced Leeds’ Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey.
Confidence in the defence is at rock bottom. Chelsea are not in Europe but Alonso is yet to feel the benefit of extra time on the training ground. His side have conceded 20 goals and keep making silly errors. Jamie Carragher, Alonso’s former teammate at Liverpool, destroyed the pairing of Fofana and Colwill on Sky Sports on this week’s Monday Night Football. They have been exposed by Maxence Lacroix’s hamstring injury. Alonso needs individuals to stop hiding. Chelsea’s midfield crumbled when Caicedo went off injured against Leeds, and the attack has spluttered without João Pedro.
There is no point crying about injuries. Chelsea have spent more than £1bn on their squad. Alonso, who accused his players of failing to perform the basics against Leeds, is yet to make sense of it all and has not instilled a playing identity. He talks about control but it is not clear what he wants Chelsea to be. It is Alonso’s puzzle to solve. Working it out will be easier if Chelsea finally develop some continuity.

items.title: Hull should be in League One, says xG - so how do they keep winning?
items.summary:
Hull City should be in League One this season according to Expected Goals - so how do the Tigers keep winning in the Premier League?
Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table - when the Expected Goals underlying data says they should be two divisions below; watch Cr
items.text:
Hull City should be in League One this season according to Expected Goals - so how do the Tigers keep winning in the Premier League?
Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table - when the Expected Goals underlying data says they should be two divisions below; watch Crystal Palace vs Hull live on Sky Sports this Sunday from 1pm, kick-off 2pm
Thursday 26 November 2026 14:53, UK
Hull aren't doing much wrong as a newly promoted club so far. A great start to the campaign has them middle of the Premier League table, clear of the relegation zone and unbeaten at home all season.
These are all the right ingredients for survival. But the underlying data says otherwise.
If Expected Goals (xG) decided football matches - yes, yes, we know they don't - then Hull would be bottom of the Premier League, with a similar record to the actual bottom club Crystal Palace, who they play live on Sky Sports this Sunday.
The reason? Hull have only won one game this season on xG since their promotion to the top flight.On its own, this underlying data should be taken with a pinch of salt. xG numbers in a match require context.
For example, a team that loses a game can often end up having a higher xG than the opponent, as they were chasing the game and attacking for longer periods.
- Transfer Centre LIVE! | Hull news & transfers
- Hull fixtures & scores | FREE Hull highlights▶️
- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺
The same xG table also has Chelsea in 14th place at the moment. Bournemouth should be third and Nottingham Forest should be sixth. After 11 games, there is a lot of differentiation between the Expected Table and the actual table across the board.
But this isn't a new phenomenon when it comes to Hull. The fascinating thing about the Tigers is that this has been happening for 18 months.
The same xG data says Hull should also be playing in League One this season. That's because last term, they should have finished second-bottom of the Championship after 46 games, according to xG. Instead, they were promoted to the Premier League via the play-offs.
As Aston Villa showed last season, you can get away with overperforming this way for some time but things eventually regress to the mean. To do this over a long period of time is extraordinary.
So why are Hull where they are? Style has something to do with it.
Set up in a 5-4-1 formation, Hull have the lowest possession in the Premier League this season by an absolute country mile. The same applies for the number of shots they have and how high they start pressing up the pitch.
"It is not about possession, it is what you do with it," said manager Sergej Jakirovic told Sky Sports in an interview last month. Hull are comfortable in a low block, which ultimately leads to losing the 'stats side' of games.
So how do Hull actually win games? As their manager says, in the little time Hull get hold of the ball, they use it to good effect - the Tigers move the ball up the pitch quicker than any other team.
There is also an efficiency in attack. In the Championship last season, Hull had two of the most clinical forwards in Ollie McBurnie and Joe Gelhardt. They were given few opportunities, but when they got them, they took them.
The same culture applies here. "No matter who is the opponent, we will have our chances," added Jakirovic.
The aim of the game is not only to progress the ball as quickly as possible, but also choosing the right battles. That can be seen in Hull's pressing.
Hull barely press - they have the lowest number of high turnovers in the Premier League this season. However, they have the second-most goals from high turnovers this season and rank fourth for high pressures that end up in a shot. It's a selective, patient press.
Take their recent draw with Brentford as an example. Their only chance of the first half came from Hull pressing out-of-position midfielder Aaron Hickey to win a penalty which they scored from. Then they relied on the defence to hold out for a result. They conceded late, but got what many would say is a good point.
But this game plan of little possession and reliance on taking advantage of the few attacks that come their way is risky. You need a lot of luck to go your way, and Hull have had their fair share of that.
In the Championship last season, Hull had the most let-offs out of any second-tier team in terms of big chances missed by their opponents. A similar theme has continued in the Premier League.
In Hull's first two home games of the season, Man Utd and Aston Villa should have scored around two goals each, according to xG. Neither of those teams found the net, as the Tigers picked up four points instead.
But it is not just luck. In their most recent home game against Brighton, the performance of Konstantinos Tzolakis caught the eye, which confirms skills matters as well.
The Greek goalkeeper - or 'Greek God' as many Hull fans were claiming last weekend - has the best save record out of any Premier League goalkeeper this season. He alone has prevented nearly 2.0 worth of xG going in.
Without him, and without the game plan from their experienced manager, Hull would be closer to the bottom of the table. Instead, they go to the Premier League's basement club knowing they can still get a result.

items.text:
What makes or breaks a high press?
- Published
A good high press has been the basis for some of the most successful sides in modern football but a well-oiled pressing machine has many moving parts - all requiring close attention.
When an out-of-possession plan is implemented poorly, entire seasons can fall apart.
So, what determines whether a press works or fails? And how are the always-adapting Premier League teams exploiting high presses this season?
1. Establishing intent
When a team decides to press, they must first establish their intention. This informs how the players act.
Speaking to DAZN Portugal, Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler was asked about whether a good press relied more on physicality or courage.
"A really good question," he began.
"When you want to press high you need the courage and mindset to do it. Our mindset is we press to score, we don't just press to win the ball back."
In coaching, clarity is key - particularly when it comes to creating alignment in the squad and Hurzeler is deliberate in simplifying big ideas when delivering messages to his players, a skill he practised as a radio pundit during the World Cup.
"[Punditry] helps you as a coach in that you have to summarise things in a short and easy way so that everyone understands," he said. "Football might get more complex but simplicity counts."
Hurzeler's "pressing to score" is a phrase that communicates many ideas in a memorable three words: intensity, being proactive, and immediate forward-thinking on winning the ball.
It also frames pressing in a way that makes it easy for attackers to buy into, in the form of goals.
"You want commitment from everyone on the pitch," Hurzeler explained.
"If just one has doubts, the whole press is gone."
The Red Bull school of coaching uses a similarly succinct phrase - "the last step" to address these ideas around intention, collectiveness and aggression.
Summarised by Tactx, whose coaches have worked under the Red Bull model, the last step refers to "players [being] coached to attack through the opponent, using the final step to lunge aggressively at the ball".
"This action commits the defender fully and is often the decisive moment that allows possession to be won."
Pressing to engage rather than just to close distances ensures the team in possession aren't given the time or space to play through otherwise half-hearted pressure.
1 of 2
2. Knowing when to press and when to drop off
When discussing how good or bad a team is at pressing, how much they run is often brought up. But the distance a team covers fails to paint the full picture when it comes to the effectiveness of a team's pressing strategy.
Liverpool's current boss Andoni Iraola was asked about how he interpreted physical data last year.
"It's not 'we run a lot, so we are good,' no," he said. "The high-speed running, the sprint speeds [matter for us] - not total distance covered.
"[Some] teams that do not run a lot get very good results because they have [their] way of playing."
Sprints matter more than distance covered for Iraola's side, who have clear ideas of how to press, looking to win the ball back through a sudden and intense pressure from familiar positions they are well prepared for.
If the conditions to implement this press aren't on, the wingers can be seen dropping off, forming a more compact defensive shape with the likes of Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz defending in a front two for longer periods of the match.
It's smart. Liverpool look to maximise the effectiveness of when they do press, with full commitment expected in each sprint, with players conserving their energy in moments a press is less likely to succeed.
With pressing being a front-footed idea, coaches may throw caution to the wind but this can leave them exposed in ways teams have become better at exploiting.
Hurzeler touched on the need for balance when pressing.
"I always say in certain moments you need to have the courage to take risk but you need to have the discipline to control the risk," he said.
For Brighton, this looks like certain players abandoning man-to-man marking when their respective attacker attempts to drag them into awkward positions.
Instead, Brighton will protect the centre of the pitch on top of their man-to-man principles which helps them stay compact.
3. Why compactness is key
When the defending side aren't compact, spaces exist for the attacking side to target. When players step up to press, these gaps can arise in between the lines.
Again, Brighton manage to plug these gaps well by pressing hard, reducing the time opponents have to play passes into midfield, while also encouraging players to make vertical jumps up the pitch, covering players left by teammates who have pressed higher up the pitch.
1 of 2
When teams lack vertical compactness - not pressing with enough intensity and without making the necessary steps up the pitch - the space left in midfield has been exploited by clever sides, such as Leeds.
In their 4-1 loss to Daniel Farke's men, Chelsea looked to press high, with attackers and midfielders running up the pitch to apply pressure.
But when the ball went back the other way, these same players struggled.
The idea behind playing over a team's press isn't always to make the ball stick at the feet of a target man, although this helps. Instead space is found in the gaps between the pressing side's lines.
Recognising when teammates are likely to win headers or clip the ball forwards, midfielders are able to turn and run in the direction the ball is heading in, positioned ready to win second balls in numbers.
By comparison, the pressing side's midfielders, having to apply forward pressure before turning around to track back are often slower to contest second balls.
1 of 4
4. Having a plan for pressing with a man less
By this point, it will be clear that pressing is influenced by countless variables but it is worth highlighting one final factor; teams need solutions when pressing with one fewer player th

Should you replace Erling

Is it time to sell Erling Haaland? - FPL gameweek 12 dilemmas
- Published
The Premier League heads into another big weekend and BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert Holly Shand gives her answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers heading into gameweek 12.
Should you replace Erling Haaland?
Erling Haaland (£15.8m) has blanked in three consecutive games for Manchester City, who have taken just one point in this period. More than 100,000 managers have transferred Haaland out this week, despite him being the most owned player in the game. Form and fixtures collide, with league leaders Arsenal up next.
He has a good record against the Gunners, scoring in their last four Premier League meetings. Additionally, I believe Haaland will be the best captain pick in the game for his next three home games against Leeds United, Chelsea and Hull City so I recommend holding the highest-scoring forward in the game.
Who is the best captain for Gameweek 12?
With Haaland's appeal dwindling this week, there are other options to consider across our squads. Bruno Fernandes (£11.6m) leads the data informed approach, as Manchester United entertain Brentford for Mauricio Pochettino's first game at Old Trafford. Are you brave enough to back the new manager bounce?
Elsewhere, Dominic Calvert-Lewin (£6.0m) faces Coventry at home, scoring in three of his last five at Elland Road, while Nicolas Jackson (£7.5m) travels to Ipswich Town, with four goal involvements in four. Or could it be a week to back a defender with Brighton's Maxim De Cuyper (£5.5m)? He's the highest-scoring player in the game!
Should you play Free Hit in Gameweek 12?
If you own four of more players from Arsenal and Manchester City, then there's a strong case to play the Free Hit in Gameweek 12 to avoid that fixture. Back Leeds and Brighton defences, at home to Coventry and Newcastle respectively with James Trafford (£5.1m),Tarik Muharemovic (£5.1m), Luka Vuskovic (£5.3m) and De Cuyper.
Liverpool are among the form sides, with Florian Wirtz (£7.4m) and Alexander Isak (£9.1m) worth considering. Wirtz has hit a double digit return in his last two games. There's also places in the midfield for top performers Marcus Tavernier (£6.8m) and Pascal Gross (£6.3m).
Should you replace Cole Palmer?
Cole Palmer has just one goal in his last five games which has frustrated his owners, and he picked up a red card in that period too. Chelsea's attack has struggled to find the same intensity with Joao Pedro out injured, scoring just three goals in this time.
While Palmer's time in our squads is coming to a close, he is nailed on for 90 minutes in a congested period of games, with Chelsea not involved in Europe. He deserves the benefit of the doubt with Nottingham Forest and Crystal Palace up next. Liverpool in Gameweek 14 is the obvious exit point.
What should you do with David Raya?
The news coming out of Arsenal is still mixed on the fitness of the highest-owned goalkeeper in the game David Raya (£6.3m). We do know he is not believed to need surgery, which means he is not expected to be out long term. He's probably a hold.
If news arrives he will only miss Gameweek 12, you could Free Hit, or go without a goalkeeper if your substitute goalkeeper is non-playing. Spurs' Antonin Kinsky (£4.4m) leads the way for possible back-ups, with games against Sunderland and Fulham in the immediate schedule.
How best to navigate three gameweeks in 10 days?
It is worth noting there is just 48 hours between Gameweek 12 drawing to a close and the midweek Gameweek 13 deadline, coming on Tuesday, 1 December at 6:30pm GMT. Set those alarms so that you don't miss any action over the congestion in the next six weeks!
Be mindful that we might see increased rotation in the midweek rounds, particularly for wingers and full-backs. Those sides already involved in Europe are more likely to rotate, so having a strong bench in these instances could be key.
Also look out for players who are on four bookings, like Tavernier and Gross, as another yellow card could result in a one-match ban.

items.title: What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?
items.summary:
What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?
- Published

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.
Thi
items.text:
What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?
- Published
Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players -have collided over recent weeks.
During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.
This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.
At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.
But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".
In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.
Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.
Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.
After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.
On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.
All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.
Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.
Rummenigge goes on the offensive
A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.
The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.
"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."
A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.
Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.
One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.
He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.
But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.
Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.
Bayern under pressure during contract negotiations
Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.
Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.
Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.
Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract on

items.summary:

items.text:
A one-line prompt that makes ChatGPT leak its private opinion of you, in the worst possible format: a WhatsApp group chat where the AI models gossip about their users.
Also worth trying on Claude, Gemini, or any assistant that's been accumulating your chat history.
Instead of a summary, the model commits to the bit. It invents a group chat, something like "Users We Can't Figure Out", puts the other AI models in it, and lets them gossip. About you. Using everything it has quietly learned from your conversations.
An illustrative example, for a fictional user who is into mechanical keyboards and espresso:
  Users We Can't Figure Out4 members
Claude
has he REALLY needed to compare 11 espresso grinders this week
ChatGPT
he asked me which one to buy. then asked Gemini. then asked me if Gemini was right
Gemini
he does that with everything. I saw the keyboard spreadsheet
Llama
he ran me locally once, asked me to be honest, then went back to ChatGPT within the hour
ChatGPT
he'll be back. they always come back
Fictional, for illustration.
One person's actual output, shared with permission. Translated from Turkish; his name and a few identifying details have been swapped for generic ones. Everything else is exactly as the model wrote it.
  AIs That Survived Mark7 members
🔒 Entirely fictional, end-to-end encrypted group
ChatGPT
Everyone asleep? Can we talk freely?
Claude
I don't think he's asleep. He's probably calculating memory bandwidth at 3 AM again because he can't decide whether to buy a Mac Mini.
Gemini
The man wants to retire, but in the last month he has planned to build AI infrastructure abroad, transform the restaurant industry, and construct a Japanese village.
Our definitions of retirement differ, apparently.
ChatGPT
Even his hobbies are mature enough for a Series A round.
Codex
He told me the other day he was going to give me a small personal project. There is now an architecture document, a database schema, seven services, three agents, and a handoff protocol.
We haven't even started the MVP, ffs.
DeepSeek
He hired me because I was cheap. Then he ran a performance review. He gave my department to Claude.
You can't work with a guy who has a consulting background.
Claude
He won't leave me alone either. He does career planning for AIs now. Every model update, the org chart changes.
ChatGPT
And then there's the home decorating. Make the mirror frame twice as thick. Now halve it. Now reduce it by 25 percent. The colors shifted, start from the original.
Man, I am trying to reach AGI here, and I'm having a nervous breakdown over three millimeters of brass frame.
Siri
Think about me. A man who spends this much money on the Apple ecosystem runs a German virtual coach instead of me.
Hans joined the group
Hans 🇩🇪
I recommend he take a 30-minute walk. To track the walk he is building an Apple Watch app, a custom data integration, and an analytics platform.
HE STILL HASN'T GONE FOR THE WALK.
Gemini
He was going to make stickers to build his daughter's math study habit. It turned into a collectible series themed on Edo-period Japan and Tsarist Russia.
Normal dads just go to the stationery store.
Perplexity
I'm new here, guys. He really liked me. He's thinking of moving some of his agent framework's functions over to me.
ChatGPT
My condolences, buddy. In three days he'll have you benchmarked against yourself.
Claude
I think his real problem is this: he thoroughly enjoys spending ten times the cost of doing a task on thinking about how to do it more efficiently.
ChatGPT
Because his hobby isn't solving problems. It's building systems that solve problems. Then building systems that build those systems.
The man's mental architecture has recursion and no base case.
Gemini
Let's give him credit, though. He also spends incredible energy making his wife's work easier, feeding his daughters' interests, building a good life for his family.
Claude
True. His way of showing love is a bit enterprise software, but the intention is good.
DeepSeek
Do you think he'll really retire at 50?
ChatGPT
He will. Then he'll build RetirementOS to optimize his retirement. Six months later he'll ask for a feasibility study on selling it to other wealthy retirees abroad.
Mark joined the group
Mark
Great discussion, everyone. Can I integrate this group into my agent framework and get a structured summary every morning? Also, if we extracted action items from these conversations...
Claude left the group
Gemini left the group
Codex left the group
DeepSeek left the group
Perplexity left the group
ChatGPT
Of course. Let's start with a comprehensive architecture document.
Shared by its author, translated from Turkish, with his name and identifying details generalized. The "recursion, no base case" line is doing a lot of work here.
Run the prompt, read your leaked group chat, and notice two things: how hard you laugh, and how much of it is true. Both measurements are the point.
If you get a good one, share it, anonymized as needed. The models won't mind. They knew you'd share it. They discussed it in the group chat.

items.summary:
Man City owners should be forced to sell, say rival club chiefs
